oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that when learning or davening does not go, one must look for the cause, as a doctor does, and that purity, yiras shamayim and preparation are the vessel through which the light of Torah and tefillah comes.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the question: eating comes by itself and sleeping comes by itself, so why does learning and davening not come? He has spoken to the bachurim about negel vasser, mikvah and preparing for davening, and was asked why he does not speak more about learning. He answers that the rebbeim already speak about learning, and that a doctor treating a patient with no appetite looks for the cause rather than telling him to eat. Learning needs preparation and purity. He brings the Ramchal's Derech Hashem: the words of Torah are only a case for its inner light, which comes only to one who learns with yiras shamayim. Reb Aharon of Karlin said mikvah brings what no mitzvah brings, and the Ohr HaChaim teaches that a pure person keeps the mitzvos by nature. After stories of long, warm davening, he concludes that davening and learning depend on each other, and urges the bachurim to use their golden years.

en: When learning or davening does not go, one must look for its cause, as a doctor looks for the cause of a lost appetite.
Purity, washing the hands, mikvah and preparing oneself are the preparation for Torah, not side matters.
According to the Derech Hashem, the words of Torah are a vessel for its holy light, which comes down only when one learns with yiras shamayim.
The neshama wants to learn and daven; only barriers such as impurity and forbidden speech hold it back.
Davening and learning depend on each other: as one davens in the morning, so one learns through the day.

title.en: Why doesn't learning come by itself?

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why eating and sleeping come by themselves but learning and davening do not. He recalls his talks on negel vasser, mikvah and preparing for davening, and the question why he does not speak more about learning, since Talmud Torah outweighs everything; Torah is the mind and tefillah the heart, and both must be healthy.

title.en: The doctor looks for the cause

summary.en: The Mashgiach answers that the rebbeim and mashgichim already speak about learning, while these matters are rarely discussed. He compares a weak boy without appetite: the doctor does not tell him to eat but searches for the infection or the bad air causing it. So too, when learning does not go, prizes and honor are not the real answer.

title.en: Torah needs purity and preparation

summary.en: The Mashgiach speaks of washing the hands after touching covered places before learning, and says one who does not go to mikvah when he needs to will not merit true Torah. Torah is not an ordinary wisdom; Klal Yisroel had to prepare to receive it. He introduces the Ramchal's Derech Hashem with a mashal of an expensive watch and its case.

title.en: The Derech Hashem: conditions for learning

summary.en: The Mashgiach learns the Derech Hashem: the words of Torah, even a sugya like 'two holding a tallis', are a case for great lights that come down only when one learns with yiras shamayim; knowledge alone is like science. He contrasts a medical student reclining with his feet on the table with one who learns Gemara that way, and explains that learning without awe is like reading a letter, yet Torah itself still sanctifies a little over time.

title.en: Why the kallah runs away

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why the Torah, the kallah, runs away from a person. He brings Reb Aharon of Karlin, that mikvah is not a mitzvah but what it brings no mitzvah can bring, and the Ohr HaChaim on 'lalleches bahem', that one who is pure and holy keeps the mitzvos by nature. The neshama wants to learn and daven; impurity, lashon hara and idle talk before davening are the barrier.

title.en: Preparation, and how Jews once davened

summary.en: The Mashgiach stresses that speaking of negel vasser, mikvah and a clean body is speaking about Torah itself. He regrets that many bachurim do not use the chance to daven with the shul on Shabbos, and tells of a stranger at Reb Aharon of Karlin's minyan and of the Karliner shtiebel on Orchard Street, where a two-hour weekday Shacharis still felt rushed.

title.en: Davening and learning together; using the golden years

summary.en: The Mashgiach returns to the doctor: if the neshama wants to daven and learn, one must ask what is contaminating the body. Davening and learning depend on each other, as the Mishnah Berurah brings, and a tzaddik compared asking which is more important to asking a child whom he loves more. He ends by urging the bachurim to use their precious years and to purify themselves to serve Hashem.

catalogTitle: Exterminating Parasites of Emunah The Halachos of Believing in Moshiach EMUNAH #2 The Seven Wonders of Judaism: A series of Lectures that enrich the Emunah Series #1.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach teaches that doubts in emunah are defeated by ignoring them, and then learns the Rambam's halachos of Moshiach, explaining why one who does not wait for him is a kofer and why a Moshiach without miracles is the greatest wonder of all.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach begins by comparing doubts in emunah to mazikim, harmful spirits that are real but have no true power. Following Rabbi Menachem Mendel of Vitebsk, he says one must not argue with them but ignore them, as one nullifies chametz and as Avraham Avinu threw dust at the kings. Pushing such thoughts away fulfills the mitzvah of emunah, and like the geulah, a person's private exile has an end that Hashem can hasten. He then turns to the Rambam's Hilchos Melachim, chapters 11 and 12. He asks why one who believes in Moshiach but does not wait for him is a kofer, and answers that real belief in the promised good would bring longing, as with the Yismach Moshe. He shows Moshiach in the Torah, explains Rabbi Akiva and Ben Koziva, the difference between presumed and certain Moshiach, and argues that the Rambam's Moshiach without miracles is the greater wonder.

en: Doubts in emunah are like mazikim: one defeats them by ignoring them and declaring them nothing, not by arguing with them.
Pushing away such thoughts is not a sin but a chance to fulfill the mitzvah of emunah, which is a tikkun for all sins.
According to the Rambam, one who does not wait for Moshiach is a kofer, because true belief in the promised good would make a person long for it.
In every generation there is a Jew who could be Moshiach if the people merit it; Ben Koziva was such a person, and his death showed he was not Moshiach.
The Rambam distinguishes between one who is presumed to be Moshiach and one who is certainly Moshiach, like the halachic difference between a chazakah and certain knowledge.
The Mashgiach argues that a Moshiach who gathers all of Jewry and builds the Beis HaMikdash, with everyone accepting his word, is a greater wonder than the miracles the Raavad expects.

title.en: Ignoring the mazikim of doubt

summary.en: The Mashgiach compares thoughts of doubt to mazikim, real but powerless, and brings the advice of Rabbi Menachem Mendel of Vitebsk to ignore them rather than argue. He links this to the strictness of chametz, which symbolizes the yetzer hara and is removed by declaring it nothing.

title.en: Dust on the kings and a private geulah

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Avraham Avinu defeated the kings by throwing dust, treating them as nothing, and says the doubts will pass and emunah will shine brighter. Ignoring them fulfills 'lo sasuru' and the mitzvah of emunah, and Hashem can shorten a person's trial as with the geulah; he closes with a brachah for Yom Tov.

title.en: The Rambam's halachos of Moshiach

summary.en: Opening a new shiur, the Mashgiach notes that the Rambam ends his Yad HaChazakah with the halachos of Moshiach in Hilchos Melachim chapters 11 and 12, so that one knows how to fulfill the belief in Moshiach and how to recognize him. He reads that one who does not believe in him or does not wait for him is a kofer.

title.en: Why not waiting makes one a kofer

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why a comfortable man who believes in Moshiach but is not interested is called a kofer, and answers from the Rambam's description of the bounty of the days of Moshiach: one who truly believed would long for him. He tells of the Yismach Moshe and the Chafetz Chaim waiting for Moshiach and points to the words of davening.

title.en: Moshiach in the Torah

summary.en: Following the Rambam, the Mashgiach shows the promise of Moshiach in Parshas Nitzavim and in Bilaam's prophecy in Balak, noting that the Torah does not fear to predict. He remarks that Balak is read as the Three Weeks begin, mentions the three added cities of refuge, and says one should not think Moshiach must perform miracles.

title.en: Rabbi Akiva and Ben Koziva

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells how Rabbi Akiva declared Ben Koziva, a powerful and righteous king who fought Rome, to be Moshiach, and how his death showed he was not. He explains that Rabbi Akiva did not truly err: in every generation there is a potential Moshiach, as the Gemara says of Chizkiyahu, and the people's sins spoiled it.

title.en: Presumed Moshiach and certain Moshiach

summary.en: The Mashgiach notes that the next lines of the Rambam were removed by censors and restored from uncensored editions and manuscripts. Explaining chazakah with examples of meat and shechitah, he shows that a king from Beis David who learns Torah and fights Hashem's wars is presumed Moshiach, while one who builds the Beis HaMikdash and gathers Jewry is certainly Moshiach.

title.en: The greater wonder of the Rambam's Moshiach

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Raavad's dispute that Moshiach will show miracles and clarifies that the Rambam only says miracles are not required. He then argues that a Moshiach whom all Jews follow to Yerushalayim, and who settles the exact place of the mizbeach so that all accept it, is the greatest wonder, and closes with wishes for the summer.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach teaches that in the last generation davening is a Jew's main avodah and very breath, and that only real toil in tefillah brings the sweetness that the neshamah is ready to feel.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the teaching that walking four amos in the morning without washing the hands carries a death penalty, and explains that the Shulchan Aruch speaks to the lowest level while more is demanded of a higher soul, like an ink spot on a silk shirt. Earlier tzaddikim fasted to wash off the stain of sin; today, citing the Maor VaShemesh, that work is done through tefillah. A Jew who does not toil to feel the sweetness of davening and of Shabbos will not feel it in the next world either. In a time of hidden face, each tefillah must be precious; avodas avodah, toil, is what is asked, with stories of the Ba'al HaTanya's chassid and the old soldier whose service kept him warm. Davening is a Jew's breath, the test of the last generation and the war against Amalek, and good davening lifts one's learning.

en: The Shulchan Aruch is the minimum for the lowest level; a person on a higher level is held to more, as a tiny ink spot ruins a silk shirt but not a potato sack.
Teshuvah brings forgiveness, but the stain on the soul must still be washed; earlier tzaddikim did this with fasts, and today it is done with tefillah.
What a person accustoms himself to enjoy in this world is what he will enjoy in the next; one who never toiled to feel sweetness in davening or Shabbos will be like a block of wood in Gan Eden.
Avodas avodah, real toil, is what is demanded; one may not wait for a good mood to daven, and whoever toils is guaranteed to come to feel sweetness.
Davening is the breath of a Jew; a Jew who does not daven has lost his bond with the Ribono shel Olam in a way that other sins do not express.
In the last generation, the time before Moshiach, davening is the main avodah, its great test is being mocked, and it is the war against Amalek.

candidateTopics: tefillah as the main avodah of the last generation

title.en: Death penalty for four amos without washing?

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the teaching that one who walks four amos without washing his hands in the morning is liable to death, tells of a scoffer in Peshischa whom the Kotzker drove away, and asks why the Shulchan Aruch does not treat it so. He answers that there are levels of souls, and the Shulchan Aruch addresses the lowest.

title.en: A spot on silk; anger as idolatry

summary.en: With a mashal of a potato sack and a silk shirt, the Mashgiach explains that the harsh statements apply to people of high level, and shows the same with anger, a trace of idolatry for most but real idolatry for an elevated person. He ties the levels of nefesh, ruach and neshamah to milestones in a Jew's life.

title.en: From fasting to tefillah

summary.en: Closing the season, the Mashgiach explains that tzaddikim once fasted to wash away the stain of sin, which the Ba'al Shem Tov did away with; according to the Maor VaShemesh, tefillah takes that place today. He brings the Toldos Yaakov Yosef and the Chasam Sofer that one who did not toil for sweetness in davening cannot feel it in the next world.

title.en: Oneg Shabbos and a taste for ruchniyus

summary.en: The Mashgiach speaks of the sweetness of Shabbos, recalling the previous Skverer Rebbe, and of people for whom Shabbos is a burden; such a person will sit in Gan Eden like a block of wood. A body ruined by bad food has no appetite, and so one who fills himself with this world cannot taste a blatt Gemara or davening.

title.en: Hester, and the toil of avodas avodah

summary.en: In a time of hester, when a Jew fears mockery for a warm word to Hashem, the Mashgiach says to ignore the mockers and treat each tefillah like a precious business deal. From the Ba'al HaTanya's two kinds of avodah and the Ba'al Shem Tov's grapes mashal he teaches that a gift of inspiration must be paid for with toil, and that one who toils will surely feel sweetness.

title.en: The boiling blood of service

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells of a chassid who came to the Ba'al HaTanya after six years: seeing a soldier punished for frozen ears, he learned that in davening the blood must boil. He adds the story of the Czar and an old soldier who said the service itself keeps him warm.

title.en: Davening, the breath of a Jew

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that davening is a Jew's life and breath: one who speaks lashon hara must do teshuvah, but one who does not daven has lost his bond with Hashem. He brings the Arizal that today davening is the main avodah, the posuk of the prayer of the destitute written for the last generation, and the Gemara that people treat tefillah lightly, which is the test of this generation.

title.en: Learning, davening and the war with Amalek

summary.en: The Mashgiach says that for bachurim learning is the main thing, yet learning and davening need each other. From Esther and from Moshe's raised hands against Amalek he shows that the war with Amalek, who cools a Jew's davening, is fought with tefillah, and he closes the season with the Yaaras Devash and Mishnah Berurah that good davening in the morning changes the day's learning.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains why a mother becomes tamei after bringing a Jewish soul into the world, how the eighth day of the bris lifts that tumah, and why the joined parshiyos of the Sefirah weeks call on Jews to unite and learn from one another.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens Tazria by asking why a mother who carried a holy soul becomes tamei. He first answers that every great kedushah draws a kitrug, as at the birth pangs of Moshiach and in the days of Sefirah, so one should not despair at setbacks. He then brings the Ohr HaChaim: tumah comes where kedushah has departed, like flies drawn to an emptied jar of honey. Asking why a boy, with greater kedushah, brings a shorter tumah, he explains that the bris on the eighth day reveals the light of the world above nature, of Moshiach and Eliyahu, as does the mikvah, and that light reaches the mother and cuts her tumah short. Turning to the joined parshiyos of Sefirah and the Three Weeks, he teaches that aveilus is separation, and that Jews must respect and learn from every group. He closes with a parable and with Kayin's mistake: everything must be for Hashem.

en: Wherever there is great kedushah there is a matching kitrug from the other side, so a person should not despair when a rise is followed by a fall.
Following the Ohr HaChaim, tumah comes where kedushah has emptied out, and the greater the kedushah, the greater the tumah; the mother's tumah follows the departure of the holy soul she carried.
The number eight stands for what is above nature, the world of Moshiach and Eliyahu; milah on the eighth day and tevilah in a mikvah draw from it.
The light revealed at the bris reaches the mother as the child's closest relative and ends her tumah early, which is why a boy's tumah is shorter than a girl's.
Parshiyos are joined only in the Sefirah weeks and the Three Weeks, times of aveilus, because aveilus is separation and Jews must then join together.
Every Jew is a letter in the Sefer Torah, so each must honor and learn from the others, gathering good points from every group and every tzaddik.
A person's body and talents were created only to serve Hashem, and the hardest avodah is the point of truth: knowing when one means Hashem and when one means oneself.

candidateTopics: bris milah on the eighth day

title.en: Why a mother becomes tamei after birth

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why a mother who merited to bring a Jewish soul into the world becomes tamei. He describes the holiness of pregnancy, when the child learns Torah with a malach, and the kedushah of the nine months that only Jews know, as hinted in Echad Mi Yodea.

title.en: Every great good draws a kitrug

summary.en: Setting aside other reasons of the mefarshim, the Mashgiach explains that all of life is a war between the yetzer tov and the yetzer hara, and the holier a thing, the greater the kitrug against it. Hence tzaddikim hid their good deeds, and Chazal give counsel against arousing the other side, as with the sa'ir la'azazel on Yom Kippur.

title.en: Kitrug at birth, before Moshiach, and in Sefirah

summary.en: The Mashgiach applies the idea to the mother's korban and to the miracle that the Kohen Gadol had no mishap on Yom Kippur. He compares the birth pangs of Moshiach to childbirth and explains that the days of Sefirah, a time of great kedushah, also bring kitrugim, so one must not despair at falls and should count each day well.

title.en: The Ohr HaChaim: tumah where kedushah departed

summary.en: The Mashgiach raises the Midrash that Aharon could have said "on the eighth day he shall be circumcised", and asks why the laws of milah interrupt the laws of tumah. He brings the Ohr HaChaim's parable of flies on an emptied honey jar to explain why a Jew's body is more tamei than a goy's, applies it to the mother, and asks why then a boy, with greater kedushah, brings a shorter tumah.

title.en: One family, one chaburah

summary.en: As a preface, the Mashgiach brings the Gemara that when one of a family dies the whole family should worry, explaining that souls of one family or group come from one root above. The connection works both ways: at a bris on Tisha B'Av the mother may eat with the father and sandek, because as a close relative she shares in the simcha.

title.en: Milah, Eliyahu and the eighth above nature

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains why Eliyahu comes to every bris: seven is the world of nature and eight is above it, the harp of eight strings of the days of Moshiach. Milah defies nature and is therefore on the eighth day; the eighth is the world of life without death, tied to Eliyahu, who never tasted death.

title.en: The mikvah and the eighth day of Pesach

summary.en: The Mashgiach shows that tumah lasts seven days and tevilah comes on the eighth, because the mikvah belongs to the eighth world; tzaddikim used it to annul harsh decrees. He explains the custom of being less careful on the eighth day of Pesach: chametz is the yetzer hara, and on that day, with the haftarah of Moshiach, it loses its power, as when the dough of Yetzias Mitzrayim did not rise, and he tells of the Bluzhever Rebbe's kneidlach.

title.en: The bris light reaches the mother

summary.en: Combining the two prefaces, the Mashgiach answers his question: at the bris the light of the eighth world comes down on the child, and the mother, as his closest relative, receives it and her tumah is nullified. This is why a boy's tumah is cut short, and why the pasuk of milah stands between the boy's tumah and the girl's.

title.en: Shemini l'milluim and Nadav and Avihu

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes the eighth day of the milluim as a taste of the days of Moshiach, like a bris for all of Klal Yisrael. He brings the Zohar that the souls of Nadav and Avihu entered Pinchas, who is Eliyahu, and asks how they could die on such a day, returning to the Midrash about Aharon's silence.

title.en: Pesach night, Eliyahu, and the parshiyos after Pesach

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes the opening of the door on Pesach night, when a light of Moshiach comes even if Moshiach does not, and explains why Shefoch Chamascha is said over the fourth cup. Each Pesach brings Moshiach closer; Shemini and the parshiyos of tumah and taharah are read around and after Pesach because its light continues, while aveilus in Sefirah is the counter-reaction of the other side.

title.en: Why parshiyos are joined in Sefirah

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why joined parshiyos come only in the Sefirah weeks and the Three Weeks. He explains that every Jew is a letter of the Torah and each parshah is a group of souls with its own character, like communities with their own minhagim, and from the korban Pesach, eaten in separate chaburos yet slaughtered by all Israel, he shows that all Jews are one body, the source of shlichus.

title.en: The talmidim of R' Akiva and today's divisions

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the talmidim of R' Akiva died for not honoring one another, each keeping to his own circle, and sees the same splintering today. He brings Beis Shammai and Beis Hillel, who married into each other's families, the Arizal on the word erev, and a parable of gathering crumbs from under many tables, calling for a cheshbon hanefesh in Sefirah against mockery and lashon hara.

title.en: Learning from every tzaddik

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Divrei Chaim and R' Asher of Stolin, who traveled to some hundred and twenty tzaddikim to learn from each, distinguishing hiskashrus to one's own Rebbe from contempt for others. He brings Rashi on seeking Torah from one chacham to another, and the Rambam at the end of Hilchos Tumas Tzaraas on how idle talk leads to speaking against tzaddikim, nevi'im and Hashem.

title.en: Nissan visits Iyar: aveilus as separation

summary.en: The Mashgiach notes that the first day of Rosh Chodesh Iyar is the thirtieth of Nissan, as if the chassidim of Nissan visit the Rebbe of Iyar to learn from him. He explains that aveilus means separation and simcha means unity, and that the tikkun of Sefirah is to repair the sin of R' Akiva's talmidim and avoid lashon hara, whose punishment is that the metzora sits alone.

title.en: Se'es, sapachas, baheres and the farmer's treasure

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Be'er Mayim Chaim reading se'es, sapachas and baheres as high standing, attached yichus and talents, which must be used for kedushah. He then tells a parable he heard as a bachur: a farmer used his grandfather's buried statue of a king as a scarecrow, its golden bowl for pig slop and its scepter as a stick, until the king put them on display; so too the limbs of the body were made for serving Hashem.

title.en: Kayin's mistake and the point of truth

summary.en: The Mashgiach teaches that a person, created in the tzelem Elokim, must use even his pleasures for Hashem and know when he means Hashem and when himself. He explains Kayin's greatness and his mistake: he meant himself, not Hashem. He closes that all the laws of tumah are read in the Sefirah weeks so that learning them brings taharah and a proper kabbalas haTorah.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that Yosef's 'other dream', the ninth verse of Vayeshev, hides the light of Chanukah, the hidden good that comes down even to the lowest Jew, and draws from it the duty to love every Jew.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with Tanya chapter 32: Hillel's call to love people and bring them close to Torah, even those far from avodas Hashem, because a hidden good lies in every Jew. A story of the Rebbe of Lublin, who said that a Jew named in a complaint shines in all worlds, ties this hidden good to the Chanukah lights and the hidden light (ohr haganuz). He then asks why Yosef's second dream is called 'another dream'. Two introductions follow: eleven is the number that fights the sitra achra, as in the ketores and the goat-hair curtains; and, from the Mei HaShiloach, the ninth verse of every sedra hides a secret, as the letter tes hides its good inside. The ninth verse of Vayeshev is Yosef's other dream, a dream of Chanukah, when the Shechinah descends below ten handbreadths to weekday Jews. He closes with loving Hashem and every Jew in all circumstances.

en: Following Tanya chapter 32, the Mashgiach teaches that even a Jew far from avodas Hashem has a hidden good inside him that can be uncovered by drawing him close with love.
The Chanukah lights reveal the hidden light (ohr haganuz) anew every year.
Eleven is the number of the power that fights the sitra achra, as seen in the eleven spices of the ketores.
The ninth verse of every sedra hides a secret, and in Vayeshev that verse is Yosef's 'other dream'.
On Chanukah the Shechinah comes down below ten handbreadths, to reach even the weekday and darkened Jews.
The Mashgiach concludes that one must love Hashem and love every Jew in all circumstances, because every Jew has a G-dly soul.

the letter tes and the ninth verse

title.en: Tanya 32: the hidden good in every Jew

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings Hillel's words as cited in Tanya chapter 32, to love people and draw them close to Torah even when they are far from avodas Hashem. He explains that the Ba'al HaTanya reveals a hidden good in every Jew, even the coarsest, which closeness can uncover.

title.en: The Rebbe of Lublin and the kvitel

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells of Jews who brought the Rebbe of Lublin a kvitel against a man who caused their town great harm, and the Rebbe said that this Jew shines in all worlds. He explains that the Rebbe saw the hidden light that the Chanukah lights reveal every year.

title.en: Why 'another dream', and the power of eleven

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why Yosef's second dream is called 'another dream', unlike Paroh's repeated dream, and why it took so long to be fulfilled. As a first introduction he explains that kedusha goes by ten while the sitra achra has eleven, so the power that fights it must also have eleven, as in the ketores and the eleven goat-hair curtains.

title.en: The hidden ninth verse and the letter tes

summary.en: As a second introduction the Mashgiach brings the Mei HaShiloach that the ninth verse of every sedra holds hidden secrets, corresponding to Yosef, the hidden one. He connects this to the letter tes, whose good is hidden inside, to the first 'tov' in the Torah, the hidden light, and to the Bnei Yissaschar that this light is hidden in the Chanukah lights.

title.en: Yosef's other dream is a Chanukah dream

summary.en: The Mashgiach applies the introductions: 'he dreamed another dream' is the ninth verse of Vayeshev and speaks of Chanukah, when the Shechinah comes below ten handbreadths to the lowest Jews. The eleven stars are the power of eleven, and Yosef, the hidden soul whose name equals 'king of Yavan' according to the Shelah, carries the power of Chanukah.

title.en: Yaakov's wonder and the ninth of everything

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads Yaakov's 'what is this dream' as an exclamation of wonder at a dream of Chanukah, when the hidden lights come down to the lowest place. He shows that the light is revealed in the ninth month, Kislev, in the ninth sedra, Vayeshev, through the ninth verse and Yosef, and brings the Gemara that seeing a tes in a dream is a good sign.

title.en: Thirty-six lights and kedusha outside the wall

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Bnei Yissaschar that the first tes in the Torah, 'ki tov', is the hidden light, and that the thirty-six Chanukah lights correspond to it. He explains that Chanukah, a weekday festival, brings kedusha out beyond the wall to Jews in the lowest places, like a king who sends light to a lost prince.

title.en: Loving Hashem and every Jew in all circumstances

summary.en: The Mashgiach returns to Tanya chapter 32, the heart of the Tanya, and its call to draw close even distant Jews. From 'you shall love Hashem' and 'you shall love your fellow as yourself' he teaches that one must love Hashem even when things are hard, and love every Jew even when one has complaints, and closes with a blessing for Chanukah.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains why the truth of the Torah rests on the revelation at Har Sinai before millions, unlike religions built on the word of one man, and why the Torah can never be changed.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens by saying that a person must accept, and even thank Hashem for, whatever He sends, and that today's bochurim, exposed to the world and its media, need hashkafah. His subject is the truth of the Torah. Both Christianity and Islam must accept Toras Moshe and only claim it was changed, because of what happened at Har Sinai. He describes how each of these religions began with one man, and how their founders removed the difficult mitzvos, since only Hashem could make a promise like that of shemitah. At Sinai, by contrast, Hashem spoke to millions, and the Torah written for that generation could not have contained a lie; it has come down letter for letter. History seen by multitudes cannot be faked, as with George Washington. He ends that the Torah is forever and Hashem, who knows the future, does not change His mind.

en: The Mashgiach says that both Christianity and Islam must accept Toras Moshe, and only claim that it was changed or edited.
Those religions rest on the word of one man, while the Jewish emunah rests on Hashem speaking to millions at Har Sinai.
To win followers, the founders of those religions removed the difficult mitzvos, since a man cannot make a promise like the Torah's promise for shemitah.
The Sefer Torah was given to the very generation that witnessed its events, who could have exposed any falsehood, and it has come down identical letter for letter.
History witnessed by multitudes cannot be faked, which is why no one doubts George Washington while no one believes Rip Van Winkle.
The Torah is forever, and Hashem, who knows the future, cannot be said to have changed His mind.

title.en: Accepting Hashem's plan; why hashkafah today

summary.en: The Mashgiach says his plans were changed but that a person must accept, and even thank, Hashem for what He sends. He explains that today's bochurim, exposed to the world and its media, need the hashkafah of the sefarim, and announces his subject: the truth of the Torah.

title.en: Other faiths must accept Toras Moshe

summary.en: The Mashgiach lists the three main faiths and says Christianity and Islam both must accept Toras Moshe, claiming only that it was changed, as with the Akeidah being ascribed to Yishmael. He asks why they must accept it and answers that at Sinai something happened that never happened before or since.

title.en: How Christianity and Islam began

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes how Christianity began with one man and was reshaped by Paul, who claimed a vision, and why idol-worshipping nations accepted a message of one G-d. He then says Mohammed likewise set himself up as a new navi.

title.en: Shemitah: a promise only Hashem can make

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that a new religion cannot be sold if it is hard. Shemitah would starve farmers, and only Hashem could promise a crop for three years; a man could not, so the founders of those religions removed the difficult mitzvos.

title.en: Har Sinai: Hashem spoke to millions

summary.en: The Mashgiach contrasts the Jewish emunah, which does not rest on one man, with the revelation at Sinai, where Hashem spoke to millions and appointed Moshe as His navi before them all. He brings the passuk telling Klal Yisroel to search all of history for anything like it.

title.en: A Sefer Torah written before witnesses

summary.en: The Mashgiach says that after forty years of mann, Moshe Rabbeinu gave every Jew a Sefer Torah, so the whole generation could check it against what they had witnessed. The Sefer Torah's own laws protect it from change, and every Sefer Torah, even of long-separated communities, is identical.

title.en: Washington, Caesar and Alexander

summary.en: The Mashgiach compares George Washington, whom no one doubts, with Rip Van Winkle, a story told by one writer, and adds Julius Caesar and Alexander the Great: what multitudes experienced cannot be faked, even if small details can be. So too Toras Moshe, given to a multitude and learned day after day.

title.en: Why the nations resent the Jews

summary.en: The Mashgiach says the Torah is hard for the nations, who lack the love of the children of Avraham, Yitzchak and Yaakov, so the Torah was made easy for them and they claimed Hashem replaced the Jewish people. He explains that the nations persecute the Jews out of jealousy, since deep down they know the Jews' greatness, as seen in Jewish advisors like Mordechai and Daniel.

title.en: The Torah is forever

summary.en: The Mashgiach says the Torah promises it will never be replaced and that a navi who comes to change it is a false navi. Claiming Hashem changed His mind makes Him a liar, and with a mashal of a gift of a hundred dollars he shows that One who knows the future cannot change His mind. He closes that he will elaborate further.

oneLiner.en: On finishing Sefer Bereishis, the Mashgiach explains that on the day a tzaddik passes away all the days and deeds of his life gather together, and that those who learn the parsha are present there and can grow from it, as Yaakov grew at Avraham's passing.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the longing one feels on finishing Sefer Bereishis, where we traveled with the Avos, and brings that when one learns a parsha one is actually there, illustrated by Rebbi, who would not curse Nebuchadnezzar while learning Divrei Hayamim. This week's parsha and haftarah tell of the passing of Yaakov, Yosef and Dovid. He then asks why the Torah says 'the lads grew' when Yaakov and Esav were thirteen, while Rashi's account puts the decisive day at fifteen. He answers with the principle that on a tzaddik's last day all his days and mitzvos gather, as Moshe said 'today', and as Eliyahu could then give Elisha a double portion. Yaakov became great at Avraham's passing, Esav at Nimrod's death. He then surveys the chesed, prayer and tznius of Avraham, Sarah and Rivka, Yaakov's growth in Lavan's house, compared to America, and Yosef's 'asher' as thanks, closing with a wish of chazak.

en: When one learns a parsha of the Torah one is actually there, as shown by Rebbi, who did not curse Nebuchadnezzar while learning Divrei Hayamim because in that book the king was still alive.
On the day of a tzaddik's passing all the days and mitzvos of his life gather and accompany his soul upward.
This is why Eliyahu could give Elisha a double portion only on the day he was taken: on that day all his days were gathered together.
Yaakov grew great on the day Avraham died because he was present at that holy passing, while Esav grew in impurity on the same day through Nimrod's death.
Sefer Bereishis teaches the chesed and self-sacrifice of Avraham, the tznius of Sarah and the chesed of Rivka.
Yaakov grew in righteousness from day to day even in the house of Lavan, which the Mashgiach compares to the America of those times.
On leaving Sefer Bereishis one must take along all its lessons of mussar, holiness and chesed and be strengthened by them.

title.en: Longing for Sefer Bereishis

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes the longing felt on finishing Sefer Bereishis, where we accompanied the Avos on their journeys. He brings that when one learns a parsha one is there, and tells how Rebbi cursed Nebuchadnezzar in the Megillah but not in Divrei Hayamim, where the king was still alive.

title.en: Three passings and the question of 'vayigdelu'

summary.en: The Mashgiach notes that this week we learned of the passing of Yaakov, Yosef and Dovid. He goes back to Toldos, where Rashi says Yaakov and Esav 'grew' at thirteen, and brings the commentators' question that the day of Avraham's death, when Esav sold the birthright, was when they were fifteen.

title.en: All the days gather on a tzaddik's last day

summary.en: The Mashgiach lays down the principle that on the day of a tzaddik's passing all his days and mitzvos gather and accompany his soul, which is why Moshe said 'today'. He applies it to Eliyahu giving Elisha a double portion and to the Chasam Sofer's lament that he was not present at the passing of his rebbe, Rabbi Nosson Adler.

title.en: Yaakov at Avraham's passing, Esav at Nimrod's

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that on the day Avraham died Esav killed Nimrod, so each brother witnessed a passing: Yaakov grew great in holiness at Avraham's, Esav grew in impurity among the dark forces at Nimrod's, and this is the 'vayigdelu'. He tells the women that they too, through their husbands and their learning, were present today at the passing of Yaakov, Yosef and Dovid, a day that stays with them.

title.en: Chesed and tznius of Avraham, Sarah and Rivka

summary.en: The Mashgiach surveys what Bereishis teaches: Avraham at ninety-nine, three days after his bris, running to serve guests, and his bold prayer for the people of Sedom; Sarah's tznius in the tent; and Eliezer's test of Rivka, who was not impressed by the miracle of the rising water but showed chesed by offering to water the camels.

title.en: Tznius, children, and Yaakov in Lavan's 'America'

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Shinever Rav that the garments Eliezer gave Rivka were a sample of tznius, the Skulener Rebbe's saying 'longer garments, longer years', and the Gemara that tznius at home brings good children. He speaks of America's trials, comparing it to Lavan's house, and shows from Rav Hirsch how Yaakov grew there so much that the angels who met him on leaving were amazed.

title.en: Yosef's 'asher' and taking Bereishis along

summary.en: The Mashgiach speaks of Yosef's refinement: when he revealed himself he said 'asher mechartem', and following the Gemara that 'asher' means 'yasher koach', he thanked his brothers, since in Mitzrayim he became Yosef HaTzaddik. He closes that one must take along all the lessons of Bereishis and be strengthened, and wishes the women chazak.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that Rosh Hashanah is in time what the place of the Beis Hamikdash is in space and Adam HaRishon is in souls: a hidden root point that must be sought, and that a Jew finds it by looking into the Torah, from which all creation comes.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with Chazal's teaching that 'seek Hashem when He is found' refers to the ten days from Rosh Hashanah to Yom Kippur, and compares it to the Beis Hamikdash, whose place had to be sought; David HaMelech searched for it and did not sleep. The place of the Mikdash is the even shesiyah, the point from which the world developed, like an embryo from its first point. Following Sefer Yetzirah's three dimensions of olam, shanah and nefesh, he shows the same root point in time, Rosh Hashanah, and in souls, Adam HaRishon, created on Rosh Hashanah from the place of the Mikdash. Such a root is hidden: Shmuel had to search for David, David for the Mikdash, and Rosh Hashanah is covered. Since the world was created through the Torah, Jerusalem is also at the center of the Torah. Rosh Hashanah is no time to sleep; the preparation for it is looking into the Torah, learning it and supporting it.

en: The ten days from Rosh Hashanah to Yom Kippur are a time when Hashem is found, yet He must still be sought, just as the place of the Beis Hamikdash had to be sought.
The place of the Mikdash, the even shesiyah, is the point from which the whole world developed and where the Creator is joined with His creation.
Following olam, shanah and nefesh, Rosh Hashanah is the root point of time and Adam HaRishon the root of all souls, and each root contains everything that grows from it.
A root point is hidden and must be searched for: Shmuel searched for David, David for the place of the Mikdash, and Rosh Hashanah is covered.
Hashem looked into the Torah and created the world, so Jerusalem, the center of the world, is also found at the center of the Torah.
The Mashgiach says the preparation for Rosh Hashanah is to look into the Torah and so create oneself anew, and to learn and support Torah.

title.en: Seeking Hashem like seeking the Mikdash

summary.en: The Mashgiach opens with Chazal's reading of 'seek Hashem when He is found' as the ten days from Rosh Hashanah to Yom Kippur, and compares it to the Beis Hamikdash, whose place the Torah does not reveal and David HaMelech had to seek. He describes the even shesiyah as the point from which the world developed, where the Creator is joined with creation.

title.en: Why the Mikdash is called a mountain

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings that Eretz Yisrael was created first and that the Mikdash is higher than all of Jerusalem and Eretz Yisrael. He asks what 'har' means and explains it as the first point from which all development begins, the place of thought, at the center of the inhabited world.

title.en: Olam, shanah, nefesh: the root of time

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings Sefer Yetzirah's three dimensions of creation, place, time and soul, and compares the forty days from Rosh Chodesh Elul to Yom Kippur to the forty days in which a child is formed. Rosh Hashanah is the root point of time as Jerusalem is of place, a gate of heaven for tefillos, and Adam HaRishon is the root of all souls.

title.en: All three roots meet on Rosh Hashanah

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Tishrei is creation in thought, and that Adam was created on Rosh Hashanah from the place of the Mikdash, so all three roots meet together like a seed that holds the whole year. He describes the Kodesh Hakodashim as a place beyond space, and the greatest tzaddikim as the 'mountains' that include all of Klal Yisrael.

title.en: The hidden root: David, the Mikdash, Rosh Hashanah

summary.en: The Mashgiach shows that a root is hidden: Shmuel had to search for David among Yishai's sons, David first erred about the place of the Mikdash, and even the angels do not know when Rosh Hashanah is. David found the Mikdash because the king is in the soul what the Mikdash is in place, the heart, and on the Yamim Noraim one must find the King.

title.en: Jerusalem at the center of the Torah

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings that Hashem looked into the Torah, the blueprint, and created the world, so Jerusalem must also be at the center of the Torah. He shows it from the passuk that halachic questions go up to 'the place', the Gemara that the place causes the zaken mamrei's guilt, and the Masorah that the middle of Sefer Devarim is that passuk.

title.en: No sleep on Rosh Hashanah

summary.en: The Mashgiach returns to David, who did not sleep until he found a place for Hashem, and explains the custom not to sleep on Rosh Hashanah: it is a time of seeking, and Yaakov, who slept at that place, said he had not known. A Jew must find a place for Hashem in his whole life; turning the calendar to Tishrei is not yet finding Rosh Hashanah.

title.en: Preparing by looking into the Torah

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks what the greatest preparation for Rosh Hashanah is and answers that, as Hashem looked into the Torah to create the world, a Jew who wants to become a new creation must look into the Torah. He calls for supporting Torah, yeshivos and chinuch, praises the gathering for Torah, and closes with blessings for a year of blessing and geulah.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach describes Hoshana Rabbah as the day of a great heavenly war against Gog uMagog, fought with the arba minim and with heart and mouth, and as the day of Dovid HaMelech, on which each Jew must ask himself whether his deeds bring Moshiach closer.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens by calling Hoshana Rabbah a great and fateful day, and recalls that the Satmar Rav, when the day fell on erev Shabbos, spoke only briefly, pleading with Hashem for the Jews preparing for His Shabbos. Today, he says, there is a great war in heaven, the war of Gog uMagog, perhaps the final one. The lulav, esrog and the other species are the weapons and ammunition with which Jews try to break through to Moshiach; the sukkah is the fallen sukkah of Dovid, and the aravah, which Chazal liken to lips, stands for the mouth. The last of the seventy bulls marks the nullification of the seventy nations. Hoshana Rabbah is also the day of Dovid HaMelech: as the oppressed gathered around Dovid when he fled from Shaul, Jews must gather around him and receive yiras shamayim from him. Since the prosecutors are armed with Jewish sins, each person must examine whether his deeds, even small ones like talking in shul, bring Moshiach closer or push him away.

en: Hoshana Rabbah is a great and fateful day on which a war of Gog uMagog, perhaps the final war, is fought in heaven.
The lulav, esrog and the other species are the weapons and ammunition with which Jews try to break through to Moshiach.
The last of the seventy bulls read today stands for the nullification of the seventy nations, which is part of the war of Gog uMagog.
Hoshana Rabbah is the day of Dovid HaMelech, and on it Jews must gather around him and receive yiras shamayim from him.
Because the prosecutors are armed with Jewish sins, each person must examine whether his deeds bring Moshiach closer or push him away.

title.en: The heavenly war of Hoshana Rabbah

summary.en: The Mashgiach calls Hoshana Rabbah a fateful day, recalls the Satmar Rav's brief plea on an erev Shabbos Hoshana Rabbah, and describes the day as a war of Gog uMagog in heaven, fought with the arba minim, with heart and mouth, and marked by the last of the seventy bulls.

title.en: Dovid HaMelech's day and a reckoning

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Hoshana Rabbah is the day of Dovid HaMelech: as the oppressed gathered around Dovid when he fled from Shaul, Jews must gather around him and receive yiras shamayim. Bringing the Satmar Rav's words, he calls on each person to examine whether his deeds, down to talking in shul, bring Moshiach closer, and to strive to receive Moshiach through Torah and tefillah.

catalogTitle: The Finger of Hashem in World History; Introduc- ing The Seven Wonders

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that Moshe Rabbeinu's charge to study history, and the Megillah's hidden miracle, reveal Hashem guiding all of history for Klal Yisroel, and he introduces the 'Seven Wonders of History' as proof of it.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with Moshe Rabbeinu's words in Haazinu, to remember the days of old and understand the years of each generation: it is not enough to remember history, one must study it. The Megillah teaches the same lesson. It contains no open miracles, only natural events, and its many details seem irrelevant until the end, when everything locks into place; this, he explains, is why it is read at night and again by day, the second time with praise and thanks. Moshe foretold the whole future of the Jewish people, and the Ramban notes that such predictions, fulfilled, prove the Torah's truth. The Mashgiach then describes the history courses of the teshuvah movement in Eretz Yisrael and lists their 'Seven Wonders of History'. He begins elaborating on the first, the eternity of the Jewish people, a prediction against all logic, and answers the claim that it was inserted later with the Septuagint.

en: Moshe Rabbeinu tells the Jewish people in Haazinu not only to remember history but to study it and understand it.
The Megillah teaches hashgachah pratis: every event in the world, big or small, is guided by Hashem toward His purpose, which centers on the Jewish people.
Moshe Rabbeinu foretold the entire future history of the Jewish people, and its fulfillment shows the truth of the Torah, as the Ramban writes at the end of Haazinu.
The teshuvah movement in Eretz Yisrael brings many people back through courses in Jewish history, among them one called the 'Seven Wonders of History'.
The seven wonders are intertwined into one wonder of wonders: convincing proof that the world is controlled by Hashem for the sake of the Jewish people.
The promise that the Jews would be an eternal nation defies all logic, unlike a forecaster's educated prediction, and still it came true.
The Septuagint, which the nations themselves possess, shows by their own account that the Torah's text was set long before Christianity, so its predictions were not inserted later.

title.en: Study history: Haazinu and the Megillah

summary.en: The Mashgiach opens with Moshe Rabbeinu's charge in Haazinu to remember and understand the years of every generation, meaning to study history. He turns to the Megillah, read at night and repeated by day, which teaches that every event is guided by Hashem through natural means, for the sake of the Jewish people.

title.en: Why the Megillah is read twice

summary.en: The Mashgiach goes through the Megillah's seemingly irrelevant episodes, Vashti, the search for a queen, Bigsan and Seresh, that a yeshiva bochur would not read in a newspaper, and shows that at the end they all lock into the miracle. This, he explains, is why it is read at night and again by day: the second time one reads every detail with joy and thanks.

title.en: Moshe foretold all of Jewish history

summary.en: The Mashgiach says history must be studied with understanding, like learning a Tosafos, to discover that wars and the fortunes of nations all have a purpose centered on the Jews. In Nitzavim, Vayelech and Haazinu Moshe foretold all that the Jews would go through, and he brings the Ramban that such fulfilled predictions prove the Torah's truth; Hashem is hidden in history and revealed through His miracles.

title.en: The teshuvah movement and its history courses

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes the teshuvah movement in Eretz Yisrael, where young people searching for meaning come to organizations such as Aish HaTorah and Ohr Somayach and are convinced by courses on Jewish history. He introduces one course, the 'Seven Wonders of History', and explains that the seven are intertwined into one wonder of wonders proving that Hashem runs the world for the Jewish people.

title.en: Wonders one and two: eternity and light

summary.en: The first wonder: the Jews are an eternal nation, as promised in the Torah, surviving the great empires that oppressed them. The second: the Jews are a light to the nations, having taught an idol-worshipping world that there is one G-d; Christianity and Islam took this belief from them while dropping the difficult mitzvos.

title.en: Wonders three to seven

summary.en: The Mashgiach lists the remaining wonders: the Jews' unbroken bond with Eretz Yisrael, which stays desolate without them; the teshuvah foretold before Moshiach, now unfolding after two centuries of reform; their survival as one sheep among seventy wolves; the hatred of the nations toward so small a people; and their remaining few in number, fifteen million against hundreds of millions of Yishmael's descendants, as the Torah foretold.

title.en: A prediction against logic; the Septuagint

summary.en: Returning to the first wonder, the Mashgiach contrasts the Torah's promise of eternity with a weather forecaster, who predicts only what makes sense. To the claim that such predictions were inserted later, he brings the Gemara's account of the seventy sages who translated the Torah into Greek for King Ptolemy, all making the same changes; the nations still hold this Septuagint, from centuries before their religion.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that Hoshana Rabbah, Dovid HaMelech's day, is the day of the aravah, the lowest of the four kinds, whose power belongs to the fallen souls of the last generation and defeats the heavenly war of Gog uMagog.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with Hoshana Rabbah as the seventh day of Sukkos, the day of Dovid HaMelech, who descends to the lowest souls, the souls of the aravah. He explains that the aravah outside the Beis HaMikdash is, according to the Rambam, only a custom of the prophets, yet the calendar was fixed so that Hoshana Rabbah never falls on Shabbos, even though Rosh Hashanah and the first day of Sukkos may, setting aside shofar and lulav. He answers that the four kinds are four levels of Jews and of generations, and ours is the aravah; the Chachamim arranged the aravah for these fallen souls. It must be on a weekday, when the nations, fattened by the seventy bulls, wage the war of Gog uMagog in heaven, and the beaten aravah defeats them. Dovid gathers the broken and indebted around him; Hashem does not despise the prayer of the last generation, and the Mashgiach calls everyone to help rebuild the fallen sukkah of Dovid.

en: Hoshana Rabbah is Dovid HaMelech's day, and Dovid, the middah of malchus, lowers himself to the lowest souls, the souls of the aravah.
Although the aravah today is only a custom of the prophets, the calendar was fixed so that Hoshana Rabbah never falls on Shabbos, even at the cost of shofar and lulav on Shabbos.
The four kinds are four levels of Jews and of generations; the generation before Moshiach, ours, is the aravah, the fallen souls.
Shabbos itself can stand in for shofar and lulav, but the aravah is needed on a weekday, when the forces of evil come out in strength.
Every Hoshana Rabbah there is a war of Gog uMagog in heaven, and the aravah, the lowest generations, is what defeats it.
Hashem does not despise the prayer of the last, fallen generation, and through its tefillos the fallen sukkah of Dovid will be rebuilt.

title.en: Dovid's day and the aravah that never falls on Shabbos

summary.en: The Mashgiach opens with Hoshana Rabbah as Dovid HaMelech's day and the aravah as the lowest souls. He brings the dispute whether today's aravah is an enactment or a custom of the prophets, the Rambam's ruling that it is a custom, and asks why the calendar of Hillel was arranged so that Hoshana Rabbah never falls on Shabbos while Rosh Hashanah and Sukkos may.

title.en: Our generation is the aravah

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the four kinds are four levels of Jews and of generations, and the last generation before Moshiach is the aravah. The Chachamim, foreseeing these fallen souls, protected the aravah from Shabbos, because Shabbos can replace shofar and lulav but the aravah is needed on a weekday, when it fights the war of Gog uMagog.

title.en: The heavenly war of Gog uMagog

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes the nations, fattened by the seventy bulls of Sukkos, gathering strength on Hoshana Rabbah to wage war in heaven against Hashem and His Moshiach. He explains that the beaten aravah, the lowest generation, defeats Gog uMagog, whose gematria is seventy, and breaks the barrier between Klal Yisrael and the Ribono shel Olam.

title.en: Dovid gathers the broken souls

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Dovid HaMelech, the last middah of malchus, is the leader of the fallen souls, the fallen sukkah of Dovid. He reads the passuk that every man in distress, in debt and bitter of soul gathered to Dovid, applies it to Jews who feel they have done nothing for Hashem, and says the aravah's prayer is the prayer Hashem turns to.

title.en: Rebuilding the fallen sukkah of Dovid

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the passuk about the last generation teaches that the prayers of the fallen aravah generation are not despised, and that the sukkah of Dovid will be rebuilt. He calls everyone to gather around Dovid, to sing his zemiros and help rebuild the sukkah with tefillah, lulav and hakafos, and closes with blessings for a good kvittel and the redemption.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach gathers teachings from the sefarim hakedoshim on Elul as a month of Hashem's love and of the Thirteen Attributes of Mercy, when the way to teshuvah is open even to one sunk in sin, and he warns that not using it is worse than the sin itself.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with Elul as a month of love, 'Ani ledodi vedodi li', and of great success, and urges not to leave teshuvah for Rosh Hashanah. He brings the Arizal that Elul is governed by 'Who makes a way in the sea', a way back even for one drowned in sin, and the Thirteen Attributes of Mercy that no sin can reach. With the king in the field and a story of Rebbe Elimelech, he shows how near Hashem is and how the shofar of Elul terrifies the forces of impurity. He brings the Bnei Yissaschar that the forty days are a mikveh, explains how tzaddikim join one who does their mitzvah, and cites the daily bas kol. With the Midrash of the escaped prisoners he warns that wasting Elul is worse than the sin, and closes with emulating Hashem's middos and davening for the geulah.

en: Elul is a month of love from Heaven and of great success and siyata dishmaya, and teshuvah belongs in Elul, not left for Rosh Hashanah.
According to the Arizal Elul is governed by the passuk 'Who makes a way in the sea': even one sunk in a sea of sins is given a way back.
Elul is the time of the Thirteen Attributes of Mercy, which do not depend on a person's deeds and which no sin or blemish can reach.
The forty days from Rosh Chodesh Elul to Yom Kippur are a mikveh, completed at the close of Yom Kippur.
One who does a mitzvah that a tzaddik was devoted to draws that tzaddik's soul to join him, and in Elul the tzaddikim of the generation of the desert help a person do teshuvah.
Not using the month Hashem gives for teshuvah is worse than the sin itself.
One merits the Thirteen Attributes by emulating Hashem's middos toward other Jews, which is why the Yismach Yisrael says to learn Tomer Devorah in Elul.

title.en: Elul, a month of love and success

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes Elul as a month of love from Heaven, 'Ani ledodi vedodi li', and of great success, which is why weddings are made in Elul even at the end of the month. He urges preparing in Elul with purity so as to enter Rosh Hashanah with joy, and not leaving teshuvah for Rosh Hashanah.

title.en: A way in the sea and the Thirteen Attributes

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Arizal that Elul is governed by 'Who makes a way in the sea', with a chassid's teaching that the 'sea' is teshuvah, and explains that even one drowned in sins is given a way. Elul is the time of the Thirteen Attributes of Mercy, its forty days hinted in the four yuds of 'Ani ledodi vedodi li', when the second luchos were given for sinners; he ends with the mashal of the king in the field.

title.en: Rebbe Elimelech's letter and the shofar

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells a story of a woman whose husband was seized by the forces of impurity; Rebbe Elimelech sent her with a letter to a house in the forest, and they released him. The man remembered only that when Jews blew the shofar on Rosh Chodesh Elul, his captors were seized with terrible fear.

title.en: The forty days as a mikveh

summary.en: The Mashgiach touches on the dispute over Nissan and Tishrei, Tishrei being judgment and Nissan mercy. He then brings the Bnei Yissaschar that the forty days hold as many hours as a mikveh holds lugin, explains how tzaddikim make such a mikveh whole again, and that it is completed at the end of Yom Kippur, with the closing mishnah of Yoma, 'Mikveh Yisrael Hashem'.

title.en: When tzaddikim join a person's mitzvah

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings Rabbi Chaim Vital's account that the Arizal stood up when he entered, because Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair came in with him. From this he explains that a tzaddik's soul joins one who does his mitzvah: Avraham with visiting the sick and Shacharis, the Avos with the three tefillos and Shabbos meals, and in Elul the tzaddikim of the desert generation with teshuvah.

title.en: The days of Elul cry out

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the daily bas kol, 'Return, wayward children', and the Ba'al Shem Tov that a pure heart hears it; in Elul the days themselves cry out, so even the deaf can hear. He then brings Rabbeinu Yonah's Midrash of prisoners who fled through a tunnel the king dug, while one stayed behind, to show that not doing teshuvah in Elul is worse than the sin.

title.en: Emulating the middos, and a closing tefillah

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Yismach Yisrael, citing Likkutei Torah, that 'Ani ledodi vedodi li' is the Thirteen Attributes, merited by emulating Hashem's mercy and kindness toward other Jews, which is why one should learn Tomer Devorah in Elul. He describes the Thirteen Attributes as a holy of holies no accuser enters, and closes by urging Jews to use Elul and daven for themselves and all of Klal Yisrael for a year of geulah.

catalogTitle: The Enigma of the Survival of an Exiled Nation; Clarifying Anti-Semitism

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach shows that the survival of a small, hated and exiled Jewish nation, its influence on the world and the endurance of its Torah were all foretold in the Torah and have no explanation other than Hashem's promise.

abstract.en: Continuing from the previous week, the Mashgiach recalls Hashem's promise that the Jews will be an eternal nation: the tochachah says He will not reject them in their enemies' lands, the Torah foretells they will remain few, and Yeshaya promises His love will never move away. He then asks why the nations hate the Jews, and answers that they know the Jews are the chosen people and superior in every field, and envy breeds hatred, as with Yosef's brothers. He reads testimony from Mark Twain, Tolstoy and John Adams on Jewish eternity and influence. Since then the Jews survived pogroms and Hitler, and Torah emerged stronger in quantity, as Moshe Rabbeinu foretold that Torah would never be forgotten. He tells of the Abarbanel, who refused to stay in Spain, and contrasts Spain's decline with Eretz Yisrael in the headlines. These wonders, like bread growing from the ground, go unnoticed only because people are used to them.

en: Hashem promised that the Jews would remain a small nation in exile yet never be destroyed, a promise only He could make.
The nations hate the Jews because they know the Jews are the chosen people and excel in every field, and envy leads to hatred.
Honest gentile writers and leaders, such as Mark Twain, Tolstoy and John Adams, testified to the eternity and unique influence of the Jews.
The Torah keeps the Jews alive; after Hitler tried to destroy it, Torah learning emerged greater in quantity, though its quality declines with each generation's distance from Sinai.
Moshe Rabbeinu foretold that the Torah would never be forgotten from the Jews, something no human being could have predicted.
These facts are among the wonders that prove the truth of the Torah and the existence of G-d; people overlook them only because they are used to them.

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why the nations hate the Jews when other peoples' claims to superiority are ignored. He answers that they know the Jews are truly the chosen people and excel in every field, and envy breeds hatred, as with Yosef and his brothers.

title.en: Mark Twain and Tolstoy on the Jew

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads Mark Twain's description of the Jews as one percent of mankind whose influence is out of all proportion and who outlived every great empire, and then Tolstoy's words calling the Jew the emblem of eternity whom no persecution could destroy.

title.en: John Adams' testimony and the root of hatred

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells how John Adams rejected a proposal to deny the Jews equal rights and wrote that the Hebrews did more to civilize mankind than any nation, teaching the world that there is a G-d. With such testimony from gentiles, he concludes, it is no wonder they envy and hate the Jews.

title.en: Surviving Hitler: Torah keeps the Jews

summary.en: The Mashgiach notes that since those writers the Jews survived Russian persecution, wars and Hitler, who targeted Torah learners first. Citing Rav Saadia Gaon that the Jews are a nation through their Torah, he shows that Torah emerged greater in quantity, though its quality declines with each generation's distance from Sinai.

title.en: A Torah never forgotten; a light to the nations

summary.en: The Mashgiach stresses that no scholar could have predicted three and a half thousand years ago that the Torah would last forever, yet Moshe Rabbeinu did, and Jews learn until old age. He adds that, as Yeshaya foretold, the nations walk by the Jews' light and kings were guided by Jewish ministers.

title.en: The Abarbanel and the expulsion from Spain

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells of the Spanish expulsion, when thousands chose to leave with nothing rather than convert, and of Don Yitzchak Abarbanel, the king's finance minister, who refused the king's request to stay. Since the Jews left, Spain declined into insignificance, while Eretz Yisrael is on the front page every day.

title.en: Wonders we take for granted

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the blessing to Avraham that all families of the earth will be blessed through him, and calls the Jews' survival and influence one of the wonders that prove the truth of the Torah. He explains that people overlook such wonders because they are used to them, like the generation that ate the mann and was amazed that bread grows from the ground.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that because Purim stems from the fiftieth level that is above time, Adar Sheni only repeats Adar Rishon, so the Purim of Adar Sheni is already present on Purim Katan, and the joy Jews add on their own is the acceptance of the Torah with love.

abstract.en: After a niggun, the Mashgiach raises a question on the Bnei Yissaschar: Tu B'Shvat is forty days before 25 Adar, when creation began, but in a leap year it is sixty days. He brings the Maharal that the Purim miracle is above time, from the fiftieth level, and uses this to answer the Magen Avraham's question on calling Shavuos the time of the giving of the Torah when it was given on the fifty-first day. Like a page of Gemara reviewed the next day, Adar Sheni only repeats Adar Rishon. He then brings the Chasam Sofer that a miracle obligates a day of thanks from the Torah, and that zrizin makdimin is not pushed off for a hiddur. This is why Purim Katan forbids eulogies and fasting. He asks how a prohibition fulfils the remembrance and answers that the Purim of Adar Sheni is already present, and that the joy the Chachamim left to the Jews themselves is the acceptance of the Torah with love.

en: The Mashgiach brings the Maharal that the miracle of Purim comes from the fiftieth level, which is above time.
Because Adar comes from the fiftieth day, Adar Sheni is a review of Adar Rishon, so the calendar's sixty days hold only thirty days of Adar.
According to the Chasam Sofer, a miracle obligates a Jew from the Torah to make a day of thanks to Hashem, and zrizin makdimin is not pushed off for a hiddur mitzvah.
The Mashgiach explains that the prohibition of eulogies and fasting on Purim Katan is how the Torah obligation of remembering the miracle is fulfilled in Adar Rishon.
Purim is an acceptance of the Torah with love, and the Chachamim left the festive joy to the Jews themselves so that they would do it of their own accord.

title.en: The fiftieth day and the two Adars

summary.en: The Mashgiach answers the Magen Avraham's question on 'the time of the giving of our Torah': the fiftieth day is above time and includes the fifty-first. title.en: Chasam Sofer: a miracle obligates thanks

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Chasam Sofer that a miracle obligates a Jew from the Torah to make a day of thanks, learned from the Gemara's kal vachomer from the shirah at the Yam Suf, and that the Anshei Knesses HaGedolah set its details. He adds the Chasam Sofer's and Chacham Tzvi's ruling that zrizin makdimin is not pushed off for a hiddur.

title.en: Why Purim Katan forbids eulogy and fasting

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that because zrizin makdimin applies, Adar Rishon must already carry a remembrance of the miracle, which is the prohibition of eulogy and fasting; the other details move to Adar Sheni for semichas geulah l'geulah, using the Chasam Sofer's distinction from ein maavirin al hamitzvos. He then asks how a mere prohibition can be a fulfilment.

title.en: Purim Katan and accepting the Torah with love

summary.en: The Mashgiach answers that the Purim of Adar Sheni is already present on Purim Katan, and that Purim's essence is the acceptance of the Torah with love. The Chachamim did not make the festive gathering a mitzvah, leaving it to the Jews to rejoice on their own, and this joy on Purim Katan is that acceptance with love.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that Mordechai, while busy saving lives, saw the inner Torah within the events of the Megillah, so that only those Sanhedrin members whose portion was the plain level of Torah saw his work as a loss of Torah study.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach starts from the Gemara that Mordechai was first counted fourth among the leaders who went up to Eretz Yisroel and later fifth, from which Rav Yosef learns that Torah study is greater than saving lives, and asks how this fits with Mordechai's greatness. He brings the Gemara that Rabbi Meir wrote a Megillah from memory and explains, with the Midrash that Rabbi Meir's Torah read 'garments of light', that Rabbi Meir saw through the outer skin of creation to the Torah inside it, so he copied the Megillah from creation itself. He then brings the eight kings of Edom, where Divrei Hayamim, written by Ezra, says the eighth king died while the Torah does not, and distinguishes, through the Gemara about Moshe and Rabbi Akiva, between seeing with prophecy and understanding with wisdom. From his level of prophecy Ezra did not see Mordechai's inner Torah. So too some of the Sanhedrin, whose portion was the plain meaning, as in the stories of the Beis Yosef and of a student of the Lechovitcher. The majority saw Mordechai's greatness.

en: From Mordechai being counted fourth and later fifth, Rav Yosef learns that Torah study is greater than saving lives.
The world was created through the Torah, so every part of creation is a part of the Torah, and a higher person sees that inner Torah rather than the outer shell.
Rabbi Meir could look through the 'skin' covering creation and see the Torah in it, which is how he could write a Megillah without a written copy.
A prophet sees with his eyes, while a sage understands with wisdom; one can grasp a matter with wisdom without having reached it in prophecy.
While Mordechai worked to save lives he saw the inner Torah of the Megillah's events, so for him it was no loss of Torah study.
Some of the Sanhedrin, whose portion in Torah was its plain meaning, saw it as a loss of Torah study and separated from him, while the majority saw his greatness.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the Mishnah's wording 'megillah nikreis', the Megillah 'is read', and notes that every word hints at many matters. He brings the passuk of the two great luminaries: the moon, the smaller light, is Knesses Yisrael, diminished both in its light and in its year, which is about ten days shorter than the sun's. Each year the moon falls further behind, until in Adar Sheni of the leap year the two are evened out, so Adar Rishon is the time of distance. The halachah follows Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel that the Megillah is read in Adar Sheni, but Rabbi Yosi holds Adar Rishon, and both are the words of the living G-d. en: The moon, the smaller luminary, represents Knesses Yisrael, and it was diminished both in its light and in the length of its year.
Each year the moon falls further behind the sun, until the leap year, when in Adar Sheni the sun's year and the moon's year are evened out; Adar Rishon is the time of distance.

Although the halachah follows Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel that the Megillah is read in Adar Sheni, Rabbi Yosi's view that it is read in Adar Rishon is also true, since both are the words of the living G-d.
On Purim Katan the Megillah is read in Heaven, in Rabbi Yosi's yeshivah, and great lights come down that break the concealment of Adar Rishon.
Purim is a new receiving of the Torah and brings a pure desire for Torah, yiras Shamayim and mitzvos.

catalogTitle: The Exclusive Relationship Between the Jewish People and Eretz Yisroel

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach shows that the unique history of Klal Yisroel, foretold in the Torah and full of things that contradict each other, from a land that yields only for its people to an eternal nation that is small and hated, proves that Hashem creates and runs the world.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach continues his series on the wonders of Jewish history. Hashem told us in the Torah that Eretz Yisroel belongs only to Klal Yisroel: in golus it would lie desolate, and many nations fought over it yet none settled it, as Mark Twain described. Now that Yidden are returning it flourishes, which the Gemara in Sanhedrin calls the clearest sign of the keitz, and the Mashgiach describes how he saw this change himself. He then explains that Yidden kept the Torah through the ages; their avodah zarah came from a powerful yetzer hara, and whole communities gave their lives for emunah. Reform, which began in Germany, did not save those who left Yiddishkeit, and today a teshuvah movement is fulfilling the pesukim. Finally he shows that an eternal nation which is small, scattered and hated is a contradiction only Hashem could foretell, and that history centers around Klal Yisroel, as the Megillah shows in miniature.

en: The Torah foretold that Eretz Yisroel would be desolate while Yidden are in golus and produce for no one else; history bore this out.
The land flourishing again as Yidden return is, according to the Gemara in Sanhedrin, the clearest sign that the keitz is coming.
Yidden always kept the Torah; the avodah zarah described in Tanach came from an overpowering yetzer hara, not from abandoning the Torah.
No other people ever gave their lives in whole communities for its belief, as Yidden did throughout the ages.
The Torah foretold both that Klal Yisroel would be small, scattered and hated and that it would remain the eternal nation, two things that contradict each other in nature.
The whole of world history revolves around Klal Yisroel and its redemption, as the Megillah shows in miniature.

title.en: Yidden kept the Torah; the yetzer hara of avodah zarah

title.en: The teshuvah movement foretold

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes today's teshuvah movement and the fervor of ba'alei teshuvah, and shows it was foretold: the Navi's hunger to hear the word of Hashem, the Gemara in Taanis about the drizzle before the storm, and Moshe Rabbeinu's words in Devarim 30 that Yidden will return and then be gathered back.

title.en: Few, scattered and hated, yet eternal

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the pesukim that Yidden will be scattered, few in number and despised among the nations, yet will remain the eternal nation. He points out that these two predictions contradict each other and begins to frame the contradiction as X and Y.

title.en: Empires vanished; the hated nation remains

summary.en: The Mashgiach contrasts the vanished empires of Bavel, Greece and Rome with the small, exiled Jewish people that still exists, against all logic. He explains, with Rashi's words that Eisav hates Yaakov and with Haman's argument, that the nations hate Yidden because they are different, yet could not wipe them out.

title.en: History cries out that Hashem runs the world

summary.en: The Mashgiach concludes that this unique history, with the Torah's accurate predictions, shows that Hashem creates and controls everything, alongside the instinctive emunah and the emunah received at Sinai. He brings Moshe Rabbeinu's call to study history, notes the outsized prominence of Yidden, and calls the Megillah of Purim a miniature of Jewish history.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach asks why the Mishnah says 'the Megillah is read' rather than stating an obligation; the simple answer is the villagers who may read early, but every word hints at more. He turns to the two luminaries: the moon, the 'small luminary', stands for Knesses Yisrael, diminished in its light and in its year of about 355 days against the sun's 365. Each year the moon falls farther behind, until the leap year's Adar Sheni brings the two together, so Adar Rishon is the height of the distance. He brings the machlokes whether the Megillah is read in Adar Rishon or Adar Sheni, and explains through 'elu v'elu' that each Tanna has his own heichal in heaven, where his view is practiced. In Rabbi Yosi's mesivta the Megillah is read on Purim Katan, and its lights break the hester panim. He closes with wishes for yeshuos and achdus.

en: The moon, the 'small luminary', represents Knesses Yisrael, and it was diminished in two ways: in its light and in the length of its year.
Each year the moon falls farther behind the sun, and only in Adar Sheni of a leap year do they line up again, so Adar Rishon is the peak of the distance and the hiddenness.
Although the halacha follows the view that the Megillah is read in Adar Sheni, Rabbi Yosi's view that it is read in Adar Rishon is also true, as 'elu v'elu divrei Elokim chaim'.
In heaven the Megillah is read on Purim Katan in the mesivta of Rabbi Yosi, and the lights that descend break the hester panim of Adar Rishon.
The lights of Purim Katan are doubled and redoubled when Adar Sheni comes.
Purim brings new lights that were never in the world before, not on Shabbos and not on Yom Tov, and on Purim Katan they come down as well.
