title.en: Purim as a new kabbalas haTorah; wishes for yeshuos

summary.en: The Mashgiach speaks of drawing Jews close under the wings of the Shechinah and says that Purim is a new kabbalas haTorah, something not attained even at Matan Torah, bringing a pure desire for Torah, yiras Shamayim and mitzvos. He closes with wishes for great yeshuos, a bright Purim Katan leading to Purim Gadol, the unity of all Jews, and the coming of Moshiach.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains Esther's words that she had not been called to the king for thirty days, in two ways, and Mordechai's answer 'al tedami venafshech': not to calculate for oneself when Klal Yisroel needs a yeshuah.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with Esther's words that she had not been called before the king for thirty days, noting that thirty days marks a new period. Citing the Rambam, he explains that one who davens must know he stands before the King, that each word of tefillah is a heichal, and that before every aliyah comes a yeridah. In his first approach, Esther, about to rise to 'vatilbash Esther malchus', felt for thirty days that she could not say a warm word before Hashem; Mordechai answered 'al tedami venafshech', and the Mashgiach compares Avraham sitting at the opening of the tent, who then received the revelation. After a remark on Shushan Purim, his second approach: the thirty days before Pesach were her preparation in purity, and Mordechai told her that her personal preparation must yield to the need of Klal Yisroel. The rest of the recording holds rhymed performances by others and a long untranscribed stretch.

en: Thirty days is a set period of time; after thirty days a new period begins, which is why Esther counted thirty days without being called.
One who davens must know that he stands before the King; each word of tefillah is a heichal, and one goes from one heichal to the next.

Esther felt for thirty days that she could not say a warm word before Hashem and asked how she could bring a yeshuah; Mordechai answered 'al tedami venafshech', not to make calculations about herself.
A descent comes before an ascent and is its preparation, as with Avraham Avinu, who sat at the opening of the tent and precisely then received a great revelation.

In a second approach, the thirty days were the thirty days before Pesach, in which Esther was preparing herself in purity, and Mordechai told her that her personal preparation must yield to the need of Klal Yisroel.
The Mashgiach applies this to the present: looking at the time, one must prepare for a great yeshuah and daven for the klal, not only for oneself.

title.en: Thirty days and standing before the King

summary.en: Starting from Esther's words that she had not been called for thirty days, the Mashgiach explains that thirty days is a new period, brings the Rambam that one who davens stands before the King, and describes each word of tefillah as a heichal. He adds that before every aliyah there is a yeridah.

title.en: Esther's descent before her ascent

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Esther, about to rise to 'vatilbash Esther malchus', felt for thirty days that she could not speak before Hashem, and Mordechai answered 'al tedami venafshech'. He compares Avraham Avinu sitting at the opening of the tent and concludes that the descent was the preparation for the ascent; he then remarks that Shushan Purim is a yom tov for all Jews.

title.en: The thirty days before Pesach

summary.en: In a second approach, the Mashgiach explains that Esther's thirty days were the thirty days before Pesach, when she was preparing in purity and saw the king's not calling her as siyata dishmaya. Mordechai told her that her preparation is a personal matter and Klal Yisroel needs the decree annulled now; the Mashgiach applies this to davening for a great yeshuah for the klal.

title.en: A rhymed poem on Erev Shabbos and galus

summary.en: Another speaker recites a rhymed Yiddish poem comparing the rush of Erev Shabbos to galus and the coming of Shabbos to the geulah, ending with wishes and a l'chaim for the Mashgiach and those present.

title.en: A Purim performance on outwardness and inwardness

summary.en: Another speaker presents a humorous rhymed Purim piece built around the question of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai's students, with scenes of present-day outwardness, ending with a call for inwardness and the hamantasch as its sign.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that the golden dinars with which Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai filled the valley of Meron were the secrets of his Torah, given material form, and that every Jew may rejoice on his hillula even without grasping him.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the Arizal's words that it is a mitzvah to rejoice in the simcha of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, who asked that people rejoice on his hillula. Rashbi was not grasped even by his colleagues, which is why the halacha follows Rabbi Yehuda; in the future, when the world is filled with knowledge of Hashem, it will follow Rabbi Shimon. Yet even the lowest Jew has a place at his simcha. The Mashgiach then tells of Rashbi's miracles, above all the valley he filled with golden dinars, and asks why the Midrash calls the taking back of Rabbi Shimon ben Chalafta's gift a greater miracle but says nothing of the kind about Rashbi. He answers that the gold was Rashbi's own Torah secrets spread over Meron, which took material form because the students showed interest in wealth; it was no gift from heaven, and when they held back it returned to Torah. He closes with blessings that Rashbi's merit bring the redemption, and with the niggun the Satmar Rav learned in Meron.

en: Following the Arizal and the Zohar, the Mashgiach says it is a mitzvah and a nachas for every Jew to rejoice on the hillula of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai.
The halacha follows Rabbi Yehuda rather than Rabbi Shimon because his contemporaries could not grasp him; in the future, when the world is full of knowledge of Hashem, it will follow Rabbi Shimon.
The golden dinars that filled the valley of Meron were Rashbi's chiddushei Torah, which took material form because his students showed interest in wealth.
Since the gold was not sent from heaven but was Torah already present in Meron, its disappearance was no miracle: it simply returned to being Torah.
Rashbi said he could free the whole world from judgment, and the Mashgiach prays that his merit bring the redemption.

title.en: The valley of golden dinars and the question

summary.en: The Mashgiach recounts Rashbi's miracles: how he drove off an official who came with a decree, and how he filled a valley with golden dinars for a student who had grown rich abroad. He then brings the Midrash about Rabbi Shimon ben Chalafta, where the taking back of a heavenly gift is called the greater miracle, and asks why nothing like it is said of Rashbi's gold.

title.en: The gold was Rashbi's Torah secrets

summary.en: The Mashgiach offers his own answer: spiritually silver is love and gold is fear, and through the constrictions of this world they become metal. Rashbi's chiddushim lay spread over Meron, and when the students showed interest in wealth he constricted them into golden dinars; he connects this to the Midrash that the gold of Eretz Yisrael is its Torah.

title.en: Why taking it back was no miracle

summary.en: Gold has many levels; when the students held back, the gold turned back into Torah. The Mashgiach contrasts one who takes his heavenly bounty materially with a Jew whose bounty stays spiritual, concludes that the question falls away since nothing came down from heaven, and says Rashbi raised the gold to the level of the beis of Bereishis.

title.en: Chizuk and blessings in Rashbi's merit

summary.en: The Mashgiach says Rashbi gives strength to everyone, even the lowest, and reveals the hidden treasure in every Jew. He brings Rashbi's words that he could free the world from judgment and blesses that in his merit the Jewish people be redeemed, before a niggun is introduced.

title.en: The Satmar Rav's niggun from Meron

summary.en: Between singing, the Mashgiach tells how the Satmar Rav learned this niggun in Meron and taught it to his chassidim, and the one time he heard him sing alone while all were silent. He explains that a dveikus niggun sung too fast loses its depth and taste.

oneLiner.en: Opening a new Tanya series, the Mashgiach sets out the aim of the Baal Shem Tov's path and of the Tanya, then begins chapter one with the oath given to the soul, 'be a tzaddik and do not be a rasha', and the contradictions it raises.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens by saying that what matters is what Chassidus taught, not its history. The Baal Shem Tov brought love of Hashem to the simple Jew, while his disciples, above all the Baal HaTanya, carried deep teachings; the Baal HaTanya also wrote the Shulchan Aruch HaRav. The Tanya, unlike other Chassidic seforim arranged on the parsha, is an orderly course in serving Hashem, meant to show why keeping the Torah is 'very close' and simple, as its title page says. Beginning chapter one, he explains the braisa that the soul is made to swear to be a tzaddik and not a rasha: a shevuah comes from sheva, seven, binding all seven forces of creation, and is related to shefa, a flow of strength from above that stays with the soul. He then raises the Tanya's question from the Mishnah 'do not be a rasha in your own eyes' and brings the Gemara's five categories and the Raya Mehemna on the tzaddik and the beinoni, leaving the resolution for the next session.

en: The Baal Shem Tov taught that every Jew is dear to Hashem and can cleave to Him through davening, chesed and ahavas Yisrael, even without being a talmid chacham.
The Tanya is not a collection of Torah thoughts on the parsha but an orderly course of chapters on how to be an eved Hashem, whose first chapters lay the foundations.
The aim of the Tanya, as its title page signals, is to show why keeping the Torah is simple and 'very close', though most people find it hard.
The word shevuah comes from sheva, seven: an oath binds a person with all seven forces with which Hashem created the world, leaving no way out.
The oath given to the soul before birth is not meant to be remembered; it is a flow of strength, shefa from above, that accompanies the soul and helps it fulfil its mission.

The braisa's demand to consider oneself a rasha seems to contradict the Mishnah 'do not be a rasha in your own eyes', and logic pulls both ways: sadness blocks joyful service, while self-satisfaction leads to lightheadedness.

title.en: Teachings over history; the Baal Shem Tov's path

summary.en: The Mashgiach says the history of Chassidus is not the point, illustrating with a quip about a maskil who wanted to show off historical trivia. He then describes the Baal Shem Tov's accomplishment: bringing love of Hashem to simple Jews, who can cleave to Hashem through davening, chesed and ahavas Yisrael.

title.en: The Baal HaTanya among the Maggid's disciples

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes the deep teachings carried by the disciples of the Baal Shem Tov and the Maggid of Mezritch, with the Baal HaTanya foremost in understanding. He tells how the Maggid assigned him to write a Shulchan Aruch, most of which was burnt, and how its every word sheds light on the Gemara's sugyos.

title.en: The purpose and structure of the Tanya

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the Tanya, called Likkutei Amarim, has one aim stated on its title page: to show why keeping the Torah is 'very close' and simple. Unlike the other Chassidic seforim of its generation, built on Torah said on the parsha, it is an orderly course of 53 chapters, whose first fifteen or twenty lay the foundations of avodas Hashem.

title.en: The oath to the soul; shevuah and sheva

summary.en: After giving tzedakah to begin the new learning, the Mashgiach reads the braisa that opens chapter one: the soul is made to swear to be a tzaddik and not a rasha. Citing the Ramban, he explains that shevuah comes from sheva, the seven forces of creation, so an oath binds a person with all of creation and all his seven middos.

title.en: An oath that gives strength; lashon hakodesh

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks what an oath the soul forgets can accomplish, and answers that its impression stays and gives strength, as Avraham's oath gave Eliezer strength on his mission. He then explains that lashon hakodesh, unlike arbitrary languages, reveals the meaning of things in their words, as shulchan comes from 'sent'.

title.en: Shevuah and shefa: strength from above

summary.en: Since beis and pei, letters of the lips, interchange, the Mashgiach links shevuah with shefa, showing the class a white beis inside a written pei. The oath is a flow of strength from above that accompanies the soul on its individual mission; he explains hashpa'ah through a slanted roof that lets rain flow down, as for a mikveh.

title.en: Seven in avodas Hashem; an oath with no escape

summary.en: The Mashgiach shows that spiritual empowerment comes in sevens: the seven blessings of Krias Shema, the Sheva Brachos, the seven blessings of the Shabbos Shemoneh Esrei. Since 'naaseh adam' made man contain all of creation, an oath leaves no opening to escape, which is why even one suspected about money is not suspected about an oath.

title.en: The contradiction: rasha in one's own eyes?

summary.en: The Mashgiach presents the Tanya's question: the Mishnah says not to be a rasha in one's own eyes, and logic too pulls both ways, since sadness prevents serving Hashem with joy while feeling good leads to lightheadedness. He begins the answer with the Gemara in Berachos listing five kinds of people, from the complete tzaddik to the beinoni.

title.en: Raya Mehemna: the ra subordinate; three judges

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains the Raya Mehemna on Mishpatim: a 'tzaddik v'ra lo' has some bad in him, but it is subordinate to the good. He describes the inner tribunal of yetzer tov and yetzer hara, where the tzaddik hears only the good judge, the rasha only the bad, and the beinoni both, and brings Rabbah who called himself a beinoni, leaving the reconciliation of these Gemaras for the next session.

oneLiner.en: Speaking to children on Lag BaOmer, the Mashgiach teaches that Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai brought friendship into the world, and that when Jewish children are friends, learn Torah and daven, Moshiach comes and even the wild animals become friends of the Jews.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach asks the children whether they want to hear what will be when Moshiach comes, and describes the prophecy of Yeshayahu: the wolf, tiger and lion will live in peace with the lamb, the kid and the calf, and nothing will harm anyone. He then explains Lag BaOmer: Rabbi Akiva's students died because they were not good friends to one another, but through Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai peace came among the students. When Jewish children are friends and help each other, Moshiach comes and the animals too become friends of the Jews. Jews today need a great salvation from enemies who surround them, and the custom of shooting bow and arrow on Lag BaOmer recalls Yaakov Avinu's sword and bow, which Onkelos renders as his tefillos. The Mashgiach tells the children that Rabbi Shimon is present and blesses them, and leads them in saying Shema Yisrael.

en: When Moshiach comes, as Yeshayahu prophesies, the wild animals will live in peace with the gentle ones and nothing will harm anyone.
Rabbi Akiva's students died because they were not good friends to one another.
On Lag BaOmer, through Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, peace and friendship came into the world.
When Jewish children are friends with one another, Moshiach comes and even the animals become friends of the Jews.
The bow and arrow of Lag BaOmer stand for Torah and tefillah, like Yaakov Avinu's bow, which Onkelos renders as his tefillos.

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes to the children Yeshayahu's prophecy of peace among the animals when Moshiach comes, then explains that Rabbi Akiva's students died for lack of friendship and that Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai brought peace among them. When Jewish children are friends, he says, Moshiach comes and the animals become friends too.

title.en: The bow of Torah and tefillah

summary.en: The Mashgiach says Jews need a great salvation from the enemies around them, explains the Lag BaOmer custom of bow and arrow through Yaakov Avinu's bow, which Onkelos renders as tefillah, and tells the children that Rabbi Shimon is present and blesses them. He leads them in Shema Yisrael and prays for Moshiach.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that Chanukah is the yom tov of hod, thanking and praising Hashem out of a feeling that nothing is owed to oneself, and that this middah must be taken from Chanukah for the whole year by thanking Hashem for every small thing.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens by tying the nights of Chanukah to the middos and says Chanukah is the yom tov of hod. He brings the Lubavitcher Rebbe's observation that on the fifth night Beis Hillel's count first exceeds Beis Shammai's, and the Ramban that the Chanukah lights of Aharon's descendants are Aharon's lasting share. Hod means both admitting and praising, and the two are one: only someone who feels nothing is owed him can truly thank, as Aharon rejoiced when Moshe was chosen. The Jewish day, davening and Shabbos all open with thanks; Yehudah, named for thanks, and Matisyahu, a spark of Yehudah, set Chanukah for praise. In the future only the korban todah remains, so one must learn here to delight in praise, above all on Shabbos and through song. He tells of a camp survivor saved by stolen bread, speaks of the hundred berachos, and reads a tzaddik's will thanking Hashem for every small thing.

en: Chanukah is the yom tov of the middah of hod, and the fifth night, the night of hod, was especially cherished by tzaddikim.
Hod means both admitting and praising, and both come from shiflus: only one who feels nothing is owed to him can thank with his whole heart.
The Jewish day begins with Modeh Ani, davening begins with Hodu and Mizmor l'Todah, and Shabbos begins with Tov l'hodos: thanks is the beginning that includes everything.
In the future only the korban todah will remain, so a person must accustom himself here, above all on Shabbos, to delight in praising Hashem.
Each yom tov's middah is meant for the whole year, and from Chanukah one draws hod: thanking Hashem for every small thing, even for what is not good.
Thanking Hashem for every detail rests on emunah in hashgacha pratis, and the Mashgiach says anyone can get used to it without being a great baal madreigah.

title.en: Chanukah as the yom tov of hod

summary.en: After an opening song, the Mashgiach links the nights of Chanukah to the middos and says Chanukah is hod. He brings the Lubavitcher Rebbe's point that on the fifth night Beis Hillel first lights more than Beis Shammai, and the Ramban that the Chanukah lights are Aharon's lasting share; hod is Aharon's middah.

title.en: Hod: admitting and praising, from shiflus

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains the two meanings of hod, admitting and praising, and shows they are one: only a person who feels nothing is owed him can thank fully. Aharon, who rejoiced in his heart when his younger brother Moshe was chosen, is the model of this hod.

title.en: Everything begins with thanks

summary.en: The Mashgiach shows that the Jewish day opens with Modeh Ani, the davening with Hodu and Mizmor l'Todah, and Shabbos with Tov l'hodos. Yehudah, named for thanks, leads the degalim, and Matisyahu, a spark of Yehudah, and his beis din set Chanukah to thank and praise.

title.en: Thanks in the future, Shabbos and song

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Kedushas Levi that pesukei d'zimra is the core of davening, and that in the future all korbanos cease except the todah. One must learn here to delight in praise; Shabbos, a taste of the World to Come, is the time for it, and song, which the Zohar places above letters and vowels, raises it higher.

title.en: Learning to thank for every small thing

summary.en: The Mashgiach notes the extra mizmorim of Shabbos and says anyone can train himself to praise Hashem for every small thing, looking at the beauty of the world He made. He adds that one can find chesed within din, as people tell how good came out of something bad.

title.en: The stolen bread in the camp

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells of a Jew in a Nazi camp at the end of the war whose extra pieces of bread were stolen by Russian prisoners who beat him; in the morning the thieves lay dead, because the Nazis had poisoned the bread. He brings it as an example of good growing out of something bad.

title.en: The hundred berachos and saying them from a siddur

summary.en: The Mashgiach recounts that David HaMelech instituted a hundred berachos a day when a hundred people were dying daily because Hashem was not praised enough, and that the decree still stands. He encourages saying berachos with kavanah from a siddur, and hanging Asher Yatzar by the sink.

title.en: Taking hod from Chanukah for the whole year

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that each yom tov's middah is for the whole year, as Pesach's freedom and Shavuos's Torah, and Chanukah is the wellspring of hod. Most of Tehillim is praise, and praise draws further salvations; he brings a tzaddik praised by the Rebbe of Lublin, who told his children he had thanked Hashem for everything, even the unwanted.

title.en: The tzaddik's thanks and the closing wish

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads from the tzaddik's will how he thanked Hashem for a private room, for his Shabbos clothes, for a snuff box that fell without opening and glasses that fell without breaking, out of emunah that everything comes from Hashem. He closes that one should take this hod from Chanukah, thank for everything, and get used to it, and wishes for the geulah.

catalogTitle: ביאור מהות צדיק רשע ובינוני. ארבע קליפות הטמאות. גוף ישראל מקליפות נוגה.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains, through the opening questions of Tanya chapter one, that tzaddik, beinoni and rasha are defined by whether the yetzer hara still lives in a person, and then begins the teaching of the two souls of every Jew and the four klipos, the body of a Jew coming from klipas nogah.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach reads the Tanya's questions: how Iyov could say Hashem created tzaddikim and reshaim when the angel never announces it before birth; how anyone can be a beinoni if a sinner is a rasha at the moment he sins; and how Rabbah could call himself a beinoni. He shows that counting mitzvos and aveiros is only a label for judgment on Rosh Hashanah, like the 'tzaddik' and 'rasha' of a din Torah. The true definition is the three judges: a tzaddik has killed his yetzer hara, as David HaMelech said his heart was empty; a rasha hears only the yetzer hara; a beinoni hears both. He then speaks of the rare tzaddikim placed in each generation, of gilgulim, and tells the Yismach Moshe's memories. Finally he begins the two souls, explaining klipah through the four shells of a walnut, the fourth, nogah, being the body of a Jew that can become holy.

en: Calling a person tzaddik, beinoni or rasha by his majority of mitzvos or aveiros is only a convenient label for how he is judged on Rosh Hashanah, not what he is in essence.

Every person has two judges in his heart, the yetzer tov and the yetzer hara, and Hashem decides; a tzaddik has rendered his yetzer hara powerless, a rasha hears only the yetzer hara, and a beinoni hears both and must choose.
Rabbah knew he had never sinned, yet considered himself a beinoni because the yetzer hara was still there and he had to guard against it.
True tzaddikim are few; Hashem placed them in every generation as its leaders, and some are sent down again not to repair anything but for the sake of their generation.
Every Jew has two souls, one from the side of klipah and sitra achra, clothed in the blood, which is the animal life he shares with every creature.
Of the four klipos, the fourth, klipas nogah, is like the edible skin of a walnut kernel; the body of a Jew comes from it and can be turned to holiness.

title.en: The Tanya's questions on tzaddik and beinoni

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads the Tanya's questions: how Iyov could say Hashem created tzaddikim and reshaim when the angel does not announce it before birth, and how anyone can be a beinoni if a sinner is a rasha while sinning. He asks how Rabbah, whom the Angel of Death could not approach while he learned, could call himself a beinoni, and adds that even one who fails to rebuke others or neglects learning Torah is called a rasha.

title.en: Counting mitzvos is only a label for judgment

summary.en: The Mashgiach concludes that the childhood measure of mitzvos against aveiros cannot define these levels. He brings the Gemara in Rosh Hashanah about the three books and explains that the terms there are only for judgment, like the 'tzaddik' and 'rasha' of a din Torah, who are named only for that one case.

title.en: Three judges: the true definitions

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara that the yetzer tov judges tzaddikim, the yetzer hara judges reshaim, and both judge beinonim, and builds the picture of three judges with Hashem deciding. A tzaddik like David HaMelech has killed his yetzer hara, a rasha like Pharaoh has lost his yetzer tov, and a beinoni hears both; this is why Rabbah thought himself a beinoni. He explains 'my heart is a chalal within me' as an empty chamber of the heart.

title.en: Few tzaddikim, beinonim and gilgulim

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that real tzaddikim are few, placed in every generation, the 'tzaddik yesod olam' with thirty-six beneath him, and they have no choice; most people are beinonim even if they count as tzaddikim on Rosh Hashanah. He speaks of souls returning in new gilgulim, brings the Lechovitcher's reading of 'one who sleeps in the cemetery', and explains that great tzaddikim come down for their generation and remember earlier lives, while others forget so that their choice remains.

title.en: The Yismach Moshe remembers his gilgulim

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells, as written by the Yitav Lev, that his grandfather the Yismach Moshe remembered being a sheep of Yaakov Avinu, showed a mark from his staff and remembered his niggun, and remembered being in the desert at the dispute of Korach, where he was neutral. He explains that Korach was a great tzaddik who made a small mistake, and that tzaddikim remember because they have no choice to lose.

title.en: Sent down without choice; a question on gilgulim

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells that the Apter Rav remembered serving in the Beis HaMikdash, and says some are sent down as tzaddikim without choice and some as reshaim without choice, while the general population can go either way; the few tzaddikim are leaders for those who want to be honest Jews. He sums up that the Tanya's questions show the levels are not yet understood, and answers a listener's question about gilgulim and those without a share in the World to Come by recommending Takanas HaShavim.

title.en: Two souls and the four shells of the walnut

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads that, following Rav Chaim Vital, every Jew has two souls, learned from the plural 'neshamos', the first from the side of klipah. He explains klipah through the walnut of 'el ginas egoz', with its four shells, and says the world, created through the four letters of Hashem's Name, has shells to break through, like the four barriers Yechezkel passed in his vision and the keruvim guarding the Tree of Life.

title.en: Kedushah and the other side

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the world has two sides, kedushah and tumah, and one cannot stand in both. He brings Rashi that kedoshim means separated, and 'al tigshu el isha' with Targum Onkelos's 'side', and the Kotzker's lesson that one indulging in desires cannot expect to understand Torah; therefore what is not holy is called the sitra achra, the other side.

title.en: Klipas nogah, the blood and the animal soul

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the fourth klipah, nogah, is like the edible skin of the kernel and like the priah of the milah, a shell that can become holy, and the body of a Jew is from it. The first soul is clothed in the blood, which carries life as in every animal, with the four bad traits; he sums up that a Jew has a yetzer hara, his biological being, and a yetzer tov that lets him resist his desires, which no animal can do.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach reads the lean cows in Pharaoh's dream standing in astonishment beside the fat ones as the sitra achra, and Hashem Himself, marveling at the Jewish soul's mesiras nefesh, seen at Chanukah, in the Alter Rebbe and the Rebbes of Lubavitch, and in the shluchim of today.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach asks why the lean cows in Pharaoh's dream first stood beside the fat ones before swallowing them, and why Pharaoh left this out when he retold the dream. With Rav Shimshon Raphael Hirsch's reading of 'our feet stood in your gates, Yerushalayim' he explains standing as being frozen in wonder. The fat cows are the G-dly soul with its seven holy middos, the lean ones the animal soul; even when the holy soul seems swallowed, the sitra achra stands amazed before it, and Hashem Himself marvels, as the Gemara brings from Zechariah. Pharaoh, ashamed, hid this. At Chanukah the Jews felt the loss of Torah as a true tzarah and gave their lives, and so the Rambam calls the mitzvah very dear, like Avraham's milah that came through pain. The Mashgiach ends with the mesiras nefesh of the Alter Rebbe, the Lubavitcher Rebbes and the shluchim.

en: The fat cows are the G-dly soul with its seven holy middos, and the lean cows are the animal soul with its seven middos, which can swallow the holy soul into exile.
The lean cows' standing is the sitra achra stopping in astonishment before the greatness of a Jewish soul, which it cannot truly swallow.
Hashem Himself marvels at how Jews withstood the exile, as the Gemara brings from the passuk in Zechariah 'it will also be wondrous in My eyes'.
Pharaoh left the standing out of his retelling out of shame, and his claim that the swallowed cows could not be recognized is a lie: the Jewish soul remains and acts.

At Chanukah the Jews felt the loss of Torah and mitzvos as a real tzarah and gave their lives for it; therefore the Rambam calls Chanukah a very dear mitzvah, as a mitzvah that comes through pain is dear.
The Alter Rebbe and all the Rebbes of Lubavitch gave their lives for Chassidus, and the last Rebbe's shluchim continue that mesiras nefesh, at which the world and Hashem marvel.

title.en: Why the lean cows stood still

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why the starving cows in Pharaoh's dream stood beside the fat ones instead of swallowing them at once, and why Pharaoh omitted this when retelling the dream. He brings Rav Shimshon Raphael Hirsch's explanation that 'our feet stood in your gates, Yerushalayim' means being frozen in awe.

title.en: The animal soul stands amazed

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains the fat cows as the G-dly soul and the lean ones as the animal soul, and says that the sitra achra, and Hashem Himself as the Gemara brings from Zechariah, marvel at the Jewish soul surviving in exile. Pharaoh hid this out of shame and falsely claimed the swallowed cows left no trace.

title.en: Chanukah: a tzarah only Jews feel

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes the Greeks' decrees against Torah: a gentile wonders what kind of tzarah that is, but for Jews it was a true tzarah, and they gave their lives, so Hashem marveled and brought the salvation and the Chanukah lights. He explains the Rambam's 'very dear mitzvah' through Rashi on Avraham's oath by the milah, which came through pain.

title.en: Mesiras nefesh of Lubavitch and the shluchim

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells of the Alter Rebbe and all the Lubavitcher Rebbes giving their lives for Chassidus, the Rayatz demanding mesiras nefesh of his chassidim, and the last Rebbe's shluchim, four thousand of whom were recently photographed at 770. The world and Hashem marvel, and he closes with a wish for the Geulah, when the world will marvel at how Jews endured the exile.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach contrasts the light of Shabbos, which lifts souls upward, with the light of Chanukah, which descends to the lowest places, and sees in this the path of the Chabad Rebbes.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the pairs Hashem set in the world, holiness against its opposite, light against darkness, day against night, inside against outside, and notes that the Chanukah light belongs to night, darkness and the public domain. He brings the Midrash of Yaakov's ladder, where Yaakov saw the angels of the kingdoms rise and fall and Edom rise without end, and asks how the Midrash can say Yaakov did not believe. He contrasts the Shabbos light, which raises a Jew upward, with the Chanukah light, which can kindle even the 'disqualified oils'. Yaakov is the aspect of Shabbos, but some souls bound to him cannot hold on to it; for their sake Yaakov asked that the Shechinah come down below ten, and this became Chanukah. The Mashgiach applies this to the Alter Rebbe, who raised his chassidim, and to the later Chabad Rebbes, who went down to the lowest places.

en: The Chanukah light belongs to the side of night, darkness and the public domain, unlike the Menorah of the Beis HaMikdash.
Shabbos is the highest point in time and lifts a Jew upward, but some fallen souls cannot hold on to it.
What Shabbos cannot kindle, Chanukah can: the 'disqualified oils' not lit on Shabbos are lit on Chanukah.
For the sake of the souls who cannot rise with him, Yaakov asked that the Shechinah come down to them, below ten, and from this came Chanukah.
The Alter Rebbe lifted his chassidim upward, like Shabbos, while the later Chabad Rebbes went down with the Chanukah light to the lowest places to raise Jews.

title.en: Chanukah's light and Yaakov's ladder

summary.en: The Mashgiach lists the pairs of holiness and its opposite and shows that the Chanukah light belongs to night, darkness and the outside. He brings the Midrash of Yaakov's ladder and the angels of the kingdoms, and asks how the Midrash can say that Yaakov, the root of bitachon, did not believe.

title.en: The Shabbos light and the Chanukah light

summary.en: The Mashgiach contrasts the Shabbos candle, inside and above ten, with the Chanukah candle, outside and below ten, and brings the Me'or Einayim that the oils not lit on Shabbos are lit on Chanukah. He explains that Yaakov is the aspect of Shabbos, the trunk from which the twelve tribes branch out, and that some fallen souls cannot hold on to Shabbos to rise with it.

title.en: Yaakov's plea brings down the Shechinah

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Yaakov saw the souls bound to him that had fallen to the side of Esav and could not believe, and that this is the meaning of the Midrash's 'he did not believe'. Yaakov refused to go up alone and asked that the Shechinah come down below ten; 'Hashem stood over him', and Hashem promised there would be a Chanukah.

title.en: The Alter Rebbe's Shabbos and Chabad's Chanukah

summary.en: The Mashgiach says the Alter Rebbe raised his chassidim to lofty levels, and tells of Reb Avraham Zuskin, whom he saw davening on Shabbos with tears for hours. He then says the later Chabad Rebbes did the opposite, going down with the Chanukah light through shluchim to Jews with no Jewish education, and closes with a tefillah that Jews spread chassidus and be redeemed.

oneLiner.en: On Zos Chanukah the Mashgiach teaches that the mizbe'ach and the Beis HaMikdash stand on unity among Jews, and that forgiving one another brings miracles and the final redemption.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with a Zohar on Parshas Mikeitz: Rabbi Abba saw a man saved by two miracles, a snake killed beside him and a ledge that collapsed just after he left it. The man explained that he always forgave those who wronged him and even did them favors, and Rabbi Abba said his deeds were greater than Yosef's. The Mashgiach then turns to the reading of Zos Chanukah and asks why the Torah totals the nesi'im's offerings, which any child could add up. He answers that the mizbe'ach stands on achdus, as the Maharal says; the shared wagons broke down the walls between tribes, and the total shows twelve tribes became one. He brings the Midrash Tanchuma on unity, and the break between Yosef and his brothers that is healed in Vayigash, and prays for the last redemption through such unity. Finally he calls Zos Chanukah a kind of Rosh Hashanah, a day when prayers are answered.

en: In the Zohar, a man who always forgave those who wronged him, and even did them good, merited miracle upon miracle; Rabbi Abba called his deeds greater than Yosef's.
The Torah totals the nesi'im's offerings to show that the mizbe'ach was inaugurated through the unity of all the tribes.
Following the Maharal, the Mashgiach says the Beis HaMikdash stands on achdus, and sinas chinam is why it was destroyed.
When Jews are united, the Midrash Tanchuma says, the attribute of judgment cannot touch them, even if they have sinned gravely.
The Mashgiach prays that, as the earlier exiles ended, the present exile end through Jews forgiving one another wholeheartedly, bringing a second chanukas hamizbe'ach.
Zos Chanukah is a kind of Rosh Hashanah, a day of remembrance and salvation when prayers are accepted.

Rabbi Abba said his deeds were greater than Yosef's and earned him miracle upon miracle; the Mashgiach ties this to Chanukah.

title.en: Why the Torah totals the nesi'im's offerings

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why the reading of Zos Chanukah totals what the twelve nesi'im brought, and why it says both 'on the day it was anointed' and 'after it was anointed'. He answers with the Maharal that the mizbe'ach stands on achdus: the shared wagons broke the walls between tribes and the total of a hundred and twenty is a new sum of one united people. He adds the Midrash Tanchuma that judgment cannot touch Jews when they are united.

title.en: Yosef's brothers and the prayer for unity

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings Rashi that Yosef's brothers could not speak peaceably with him because they were men of truth, and shows the repair in Vayigash, where they spoke with him in love. He then prays that the present exile end as the earlier ones did, through Jews forgiving one another wholeheartedly, so that the 'second' chanukas hamizbe'ach, the building of the Beis HaMikdash, will come.

He then speaks of the treasures of Chanukah, citing the Skverer Rebbe, of Al HaNissim in bentching, and of the Rizhiner's prayer for mercy on the whole world.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach contrasts the self-serving kindness of the nations, whose animal soul comes from the impure klipos, with a Jew's ability to act purely for Hashem, and then opens Tanya chapter two: the Jew's second soul is 'truly a part of G-d above'.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach reviews that a Jew's animal soul comes from klipas nogah, which can be elevated, while that of the nations comes from the three impure klipos; therefore, as the Gemara says, the kindness of the nations is a sin, done for themselves. He shows the opposite with Yaakov's seven years for Rachel, which seemed like a few days because his love was spiritual, like a tzaddik's longing for a mitzvah. Love for a thing one consumes is really self-love, and even tzedakah or martyrdom can be for oneself; a Jew can lift his compassion and even his eating to be for Hashem. Answering a question, he digresses to the Zohar: Rachel is the aspect of Yovel, of return and redemption, explaining theft, the Hebrew servant, Shabbos, Chanukah, Yaakov's grief at Rachel's death and Migdal Eder. Finally he opens Tanya chapter two: the Jewish soul is G-dliness 'mamash', breathed from Hashem's inwardness.

en: A Jew's animal soul is from klipas nogah and can be elevated; that of the nations is from the three impure klipos and cannot, so their kindness is done for themselves.
Yaakov's seven years seemed like a few days because his love for Rachel was spiritual, like a tzaddik's longing to do a mitzvah.
Most human love is self-love; even giving tzedakah or giving one's life can be for one's own satisfaction or fame.
A Jew's compassion also comes from the animal soul, but he can work on himself to act purely for Hashem, and even his eating can be elevated.
Following the Zohar, Rachel is the aspect of Yovel, return to the root and redemption, which is why Yaakov worked seven years for her.
The Tanya's word 'mamash' is exact: the second soul of a Jew is actual G-dliness, breathed from Hashem's inwardness.

title.en: Klipas nogah and the kindness of the nations

summary.en: The Mashgiach reviews that a Jew's animal soul is from klipas nogah, which can be raised to good, while that of the nations is from the three impure klipos, as in the Eitz Chaim. He brings the Gemara in Bava Basra that the kindness of the nations is a sin, since they cannot act purely for Hashem.

title.en: Yaakov's seven years for Rachel

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why seven years of waiting seemed to Yaakov like a few days, and explains that his love for Rachel was spiritual, like Rav Nachum of Chernobyl longing for the esrog or a person building a sukkah. Yaakov's kiss was like kissing tefillin.

title.en: Loving oneself versus loving Hashem

summary.en: With the man who 'loves chicken', the Mashgiach shows that most love is self-love. He contrasts tzedakah given out of love of Hashem with giving to calm one's own feelings or to win honor, explains 'chesed le'umim chatas' this way, and says a Jew can lift his compassion to be purely for Hashem.

title.en: Exceptions, and elevating a steak

summary.en: Answering a question, the Mashgiach says exceptional individuals among the nations carry sparks of Jewish souls, as with converts. He explains that a Jew's eating, from klipas nogah, can be elevated when done for Hashem or used for learning, while forbidden food cannot be raised until the days of Moshiach.

title.en: Rachel and Yovel: everything returns to its root

summary.en: Bringing the Zohar on Yaakov's seven years, the Mashgiach explains Yovel as return to the root: every person's portion holds sparks only he can elevate. A thief takes another's portion, and a Hebrew servant, who lost the forty days of Torah, falls to a shifchah; Shabbos returns him, and Yovel frees even one who wishes to stay.

title.en: Chanukah as Yovel; Rachel and Moshiach

summary.en: Going off on a tangent before Chanukah, the Mashgiach explains with the Me'or Einayim that wicks and oils not lit on Shabbos are lit on Chanukah: souls Shabbos cannot lift, Chanukah, the eighth like Yovel, can. Rachel, who unites Klal Yisrael, is the shofar of Moshiach and the ingathering, buried near Beis Lechem, and Yaakov worked seven years to reach Yovel through her.

title.en: Rachel's death and Migdal Eder

summary.en: The Mashgiach notes that Yaakov himself offered the seven years, and brings the Zohar that Rachel's death was his greatest suffering: he felt the geulah taken away. He then brings the Targum Yonasan and the passuk in Michah that Migdal Eder is where Moshiach will be revealed, Hashem's consolation to Yaakov, and takes a question about Leah.

title.en: The second soul: G-dliness 'mamash'

summary.en: The Mashgiach opens Tanya chapter two and stresses that every word is exact, so 'mamash' means actually. Unlike the animal soul shared with all creatures, the second soul is G-dliness itself; he brings the Zohar that Hashem, the Torah and Yisrael are one, the passuk 'vayipach b'apav', the bracha Elokai neshamah, and that one who blows, blows from within himself.

title.en: Neshamah and breath; 'alu b'machshavah'

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that neshamah also means breath, a person's inwardness, as seen in Rus's kiss of Naomi against Orpah's. He then reads that Yisrael 'arose in thought' first, the reason for creation, and notes the Tanya writes 'by way of a parable' here, since Hashem's thought is unlike ours.

oneLiner.en: Through a piece of Sfas Emes, the Mashgiach explains that Chanukah opens the source of miracles, a level above nature, so that everything in these days comes through miracles, and he urges using the last day of Chanukah to draw on it.

abstract.en: After a word on the seudos of Chanukah, the Mashgiach turns to a piece of Sfas Emes. It asks why the blessing is 'she'asa nissim' if it refers to the miracle of the oil, and answers that the lighting is not chiefly for that miracle: Chanukah comes from a level above the seven days of nature, the source of miracles, which descends into time during these eight days. As during Sefirah everything relates to the day's sefirah, on Chanukah everything carries miracles; this is why even the first day, with enough oil, has a blessing. The Mashgiach applies this to the last day of Chanukah and to the present need of Jews for miracles, tells of Rabbi Shlomo Kluger and of Ruzhin on the worth of Chanukah, and closes with Chanukah as a time of pekidas akaros, also for one barren in Torah and tefillah.

en: Chanukah comes from a level above nature, the place from which miracles come, and that level descends into the world in these days.
Above the order of nature set in the seven days of creation there is an order of miracles, and on Chanukah it is joined to time.
The blessing 'she'asa nissim' is said not on the miracle of the oil but on the opening of the source of miracles in these days.
Everything on Chanukah, from the food to the candles, carries miracles, and even the first night's light burned from the source of miracles.
The Mashgiach says that on the last day of Chanukah one must work to connect to the source of miracles, since Jews today need miracles.
Chanukah is a time of pekidas akaros, and this includes one who is 'barren' in Torah or in tefillah.

He draws on the Hallel's complaint 'why should the nations say', and notes that tomorrow one can still say Hallel and Al Hanissim.

title.en: Rabbi Shlomo Kluger, Ruzhin and the dreidel

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells of a question put to Rabbi Shlomo Kluger by a prisoner let out for a short time, and of his answer favoring Hallel with the tzibbur over lighting. He cites the Ruzhiner that a simple Jew can accomplish on Chanukah what a tzaddik accomplishes with his tefillos, and tells of young men playing dreidel and the saying that what one wins on Chanukah cannot be lost.

title.en: Pekidas akaros and closing tefillah

summary.en: After a long niggun, the Mashgiach says Chanukah is a time of pekidas akaros like Rosh Hashanah, and, citing a Midrash, that barrenness includes one who sees no fruit in his Torah or tefillah. He urges using tomorrow's Hallel and Al Hanissim to ask that Jews be remembered with salvation and that barren Zion be remembered, with the ingathering of the exiles. oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that Zos Chanukah, the eighth day, corresponds to Shemini Atzeres and to the ushpiz of Shlomo HaMelech, the moon in its fullness, when holiness conquers the reshus harabim and turns it into a reshus hayachid, in the world and in each Jew's heart.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the menorah standing beside Sukkos: Chanukah, like Sukkos, has eight days, so Zos Chanukah is the counterpart of Shemini Atzeres, whose ushpiz is Shlomo HaMelech. The Chanukah light goes out into the reshus harabim, and holiness breaks into the place and the time of impurity, at the dark end of the month, in Teves. Shlomo, the fifteenth generation from Avraham, is the moon in its fullness; he took the daughters of kings to bring the nations under holiness and strove to bring the days of Moshiach, and even the two harlots, the chief feminine kelipos, submitted to him. Each Jew has his own reshus hayachid and reshus harabim, and Chanukah is the time to subdue the second to the first. After the churban, the festivals no longer gave enough strength for the whole year, so Hashem added Purim and then Chanukah as stations between Sukkos and Pesach. From Chanukah one takes thanksgiving for every small thing. He closes with the mashal of the queen who will return only if the king lifts her up, and a tefilah for Moshiach.

en: Since Chanukah has eight days like Sukkos, Zos Chanukah corresponds to Shemini Atzeres, whose ushpiz is Shlomo HaMelech.
The Chanukah light enters the reshus harabim: holiness conquers both the place and the time that belonged to the other side and turns the public domain into a reshus hayachid.
Shlomo HaMelech is the moon in its fullness, and he took the daughters of kings in order to bring all the nations under holiness.
Every Jew has a reshus hayachid, the side of the heart that longs to serve Hashem, and a reshus harabim that wants only physical things; Chanukah is the time to subdue the second to the first.
After the churban the festivals no longer gave enough strength for the whole year, so Hashem gave Purim and later Chanukah as stations between Sukkos and Pesach.
What one takes from Chanukah is thanksgiving: thanking Hashem constantly, for every small thing.

title.en: Shlomo, the full moon, and his wives

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Midrash that Shlomo, fifteen generations from Avraham, is the moon in its fullness, and says his ushpiz on Zos Chanukah turns the reshus harabim into a reshus hayachid, with all thirteen attributes of mercy present. He then explains that Shlomo, beloved of Hashem and author of Shir HaShirim, took the daughters of kings for the sake of Heaven, to bring the seventy nations under holiness.

title.en: Shlomo's striving for the days of Moshiach

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Pri Tzaddik that Shlomo tried to bring the days of Moshiach, when Hashem will be King over all the earth, and that in his days the sitra achra submitted to him. The two harlots who came before him were, as the Midrash says, the two chief feminine kelipos, and their submission came through his taking the daughters of kings; this is the power of Zos Chanukah.

title.en: The reshus harabim inside every Jew

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that every Jew is a small world, with a reshus hayachid in the right side of his heart and a reshus harabim in the left that wants only physical things. Chanukah, and Zos Chanukah above all, is the time to subdue one's reshus harabim so that even physical matters become for the sake of Heaven, as the kingdom of Yavan was handed over to the tzaddikim.

title.en: Purim and Chanukah as stations, and thanksgiving

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the three festivals give strength for the whole year, but after the churban, without the Beis HaMikdash, it was not enough, so Hashem gave Purim and then, against the Greek culture of Yavan, Chanukah, as stations between Sukkos and Pesach. What one takes from Chanukah is thanking Hashem for every small thing, and he tells of an oved who thanked Hashem even over his snuff.

title.en: The king who must lift up the queen

summary.en: The Mashgiach says the holiness of Zos Chanukah comes down to the very lowest place, and brings the passuk 'she has fallen and will no longer rise' as the Gemara in Berachos and the Zohar read it: a king twice sent away the queen and called her back, and the third time she refused to return unless the king himself lifts her up. Every Chanukah reveals the light of Moshiach, and he says one must daven to be lifted and let oneself be lifted. He closes with a tefilah that the light of Moshiach revealed on Chanukah be fulfilled and Moshiach come.

oneLiner.en: At a Zos Chanukah gathering the Mashgiach gives his chaburah practical advice on learning, davening, Chofetz Chaim and Shabbos, and explains the Chanukah lights as the chinuch of the light of Moshiach.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens by thanking Hashem and, with Yosef's words to his brothers and the Ba'al Shem Tov, says that wherever a person is sent he has something to repair. Then he offers advice. He asks the chaburah to learn at night where they daven. He describes tefillah rising through the worlds to Shemoneh Esrei and the descent of the bounty afterwards, comparing one who leaves early to a shopper who pays and leaves his bag on the counter. Following the Imrei Emes's letter, he urges learning two halachos of Chofetz Chaim daily with a chavrusa, and suggests Shabbos gatherings and using shalosh seudos. On Chanukah he brings the Bnei Yissaschar that the lights are the chinuch of the light of Moshiach, and reads the nations' outcry against Jewish ownership of Eretz Yisroel through Rashi's first comment as a reason for joy. He closes with blessings for unity.

en: Where a person is sent is a sign from Hashem that he has something to repair there and a shlichus to fulfill.
The Mashgiach asks that the chaburah learn in the same beis medrash where they daven, with a fixed place for both tefillah and Torah.
The bounty gathered in Shemoneh Esrei descends in the parts of davening after it, so one should daven the whole davening and not leave early.
The Mashgiach proposes that each person learn two halachos of Chofetz Chaim daily with his chavrusa, finishing the sefer in a year.
The Chanukah lights lit generation after generation are the chinuch of the light of Moshiach, which will then be revealed in full.

title.en: Tefillah rising through the worlds

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes how davening rises from world to world, from pesukei dezimra to Shemoneh Esrei, where one stands before the King and asks for parnassah, refuos and everything. He tells of a man who davened there that a household helper not leave, and answers that one davens according to the plain meaning: to whom else should he ask?

title.en: The descent of the bounty after Shemoneh Esrei

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the bounty gathered in tefillah descends at Tachanun, Uva Letziyon and Aleinu, and compares one who leaves before then to a shopper who pays and leaves his bag on the counter. He rejects the claim that this is unnecessary, says it is not his own stringency but comes from great tzaddikim, and asks that people daven the whole davening.

title.en: The Imrei Emes and the sefer Chofetz Chaim

summary.en: The Mashgiach recalls that the chaburah once all learned the same sefer so they could discuss it, and now urges learning Chofetz Chaim. He tells how the Imrei Emes wrote a letter to his chassidim to learn it, saying he felt its benefit himself, and thereby broke the divide between chassidim and Litvaks; the Mashgiach adds that learning it made him a different person.

title.en: Two halachos a day with a chavrusa

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that holding back a forbidden word at every moment is constant yiras shamayim and conquest of the yetzer, a great nachas ruach to Hashem. He proposes two halachos a day with one's chavrusa, at the start or end of learning, and suggests Rabbi Shimon Finkelman's English book for learning at home with the family.

title.en: Shabbos gatherings and shalosh seudos

summary.en: After asking for a refuah shleimah, the Mashgiach speaks of feeling a sweetness in Shabbos. He remembers Friday nights as a young man, when ten or fifteen Jews sat together telling stories of tzaddikim and singing zemiros, the high point of his week, and urges coming together and using the hour of shalosh seudos, which makes a person better.

title.en: Chanukah lights and the light of Moshiach

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the Chanukah lights are the light of Moshiach, and that the lights Jews kindle generation after generation gather until it is revealed in full; the Bnei Yissaschar calls them its chinuch. He then reads the nations' outcry that the Jews are robbers in Eretz Yisroel through Rashi's first comment on Bereishis, and says it is a reason to rejoice.

title.en: Blessings for unity and the third Beis HaMikdash

summary.en: The Mashgiach blesses the gathering that, with the power of Chanukah, the honor of Heaven be revealed and the third Beis HaMikdash be built, with yeshuos, refuos and simcha. He stresses that love and friendship among Jews bring blessing, cites Rabbi Akiva's great principle and the tefillah of Rebbe Elimelech to see the good in one's fellow, and ends with l'chaim.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains the Tanya's teaching that a Jewish soul is breathed from Hashem's innermost being and arose in His thought as the purpose of creation, and why, though all souls are one, there are endless levels among them.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach reads Tanya chapter 2: the second soul, unique to Jews, is a part of G-d above, as the Torah says Hashem 'breathed' a soul into Adam. Breath comes from within, so the soul comes from Hashem's inwardness, and every Jew says so of himself each morning. Every breath brings new life and a new task, which leads him to the story of the Alter Rebbe telling the Czar the time. He then explains that Jewish souls arose in Hashem's thought, the purpose for which the whole world was built, like a house built for the owner's wish to live in it, and compares this to a child that originates in the father's mind. After stressing that Hashem's wisdom is beyond human grasp, he asks how there can be levels among souls that are all one, and explains the levels through the structure of Adam HaRishon, the generations down to ikvesa diMeshicha, and the months down to Adar.

en: The Torah says Hashem 'breathed' the soul into Adam to teach that a Jewish soul comes from Hashem's innermost being, not from His 'hands', and this applies to every Jew.
Every breath is new life from Hashem, and every moment brings a different form of avodas Hashem.
Jewish souls arose in Hashem's thought first, and the entire universe was created only for their sake.
Hashem's wisdom is not a faculty He has, as it is in man; He is the knower and the knowledge, which the human mind was not made to grasp.
All Jewish souls are equal at their root; the differences are in their garments of Torah and mitzvos, and in the place each soul has in the structure of Adam HaRishon.
The generations descend from the dor hamidbar, the 'head', down to ikvesa diMeshicha, the 'heels', and the months descend in the same way down to Adar.

title.en: A soul breathed from within

summary.en: The Mashgiach opens Tanya chapter 2 on the second soul, unique to Jews, a part of G-d above, and explains why the Torah says Hashem 'breathed' a soul into Adam: breath comes from one's inwardness. He adds that every Jew says this of himself each morning and that every breath is new life from Hashem.

title.en: The Alter Rebbe tells the Czar the time

summary.en: Mentioning the Ba'al HaTanya's yahrzeit, the Mashgiach tells how the disguised Czar visited him in prison, how he recognized the king, and how he knew the exact time without a clock through the permutations of Hashem's Name that rule each hour, minute and second.

title.en: A new avodah in every moment

summary.en: The Mashgiach draws from the story that every moment calls for a different kind of avodas Hashem: with simchah at one time, with holding on to emunah at another. Life is dynamic, and with every breath a person takes in new life and a new shlichus.

title.en: Souls arose in His thought

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains 'the souls of Israel arose in thought' with the mashal of a man who builds a house: all the bricks and workers serve his first thought of living there. So the whole universe was created only because Hashem wanted Klal Yisrael, as the passuk calls Israel His firstborn son.

title.en: The Torah as the blueprint of nature

summary.en: In a digression the Mashgiach explains that Hashem looked into the Torah and created the world, so all of nature is in the Torah, and the great Chachamim learned medicine and the sciences from it. He contrasts this with scientists who only know the surface, illustrated by the question why a knife cuts challah and not the reverse.

title.en: Like a child from the father's mind

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains the Tanya's mashal: a child originates in the father's mind, which comes down and takes physical form, and so Jewish souls come from Hashem's thought, as the pesukim call Israel His son and children. He stresses that this is only a mashal, since Hashem's thought is not like ours, and that it applies to every individual Jew.

title.en: He is the knower and the knowledge

summary.en: Bringing Patach Eliyahu and the Rambam, the Mashgiach explains that Hashem's wisdom is not a faculty He has but is He Himself, which the human mind, made for this world like fins for water, cannot grasp. With the mashal of seeing a symphony he shows that the intellect is the wrong sense for this; only a deeper sense of emunah, and in prophets nevuah, reaches it.

title.en: If all are one, why levels?

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks: if every Jew is a part of G-d above, and G-dliness is one and indivisible, how can there be higher and lower souls? He answers that at the root all are equal and the differences lie in their garments of Torah and mitzvos, as will be seen in the circle dance of the tzaddikim, and then reads the Tanya on the endless levels from the Avos and Moshe Rabbeinu down to the generations before Moshiach.

title.en: Adam HaRishon, the challah of the world

summary.en: Pausing before going on, the Mashgiach explains that Adam HaRishon was the choice piece Hashem took from the 'dough' of the earth, from the place of the mizbeach, and so he is called the challah of the world. This is the reason he gives for the minhag the Rama records of women baking challah for Shabbos every Friday, since Chava brought death on him on a Friday, and in this 'challah' all Jewish souls are included.

title.en: Souls in the limbs of Adam HaRishon

summary.en: Citing a Medrash, the Mashgiach explains that every soul has its place in the body of Adam HaRishon: souls of the head are the thinkers and Talmidei Chachamim, like Moshe Rabbeinu; souls of the heart are the people of feeling and tefillah and the poets, like David HaMelech; then the hands and the feet. Every generation contains the whole structure, from its heads to its heels.

title.en: From the dor hamidbar to the heels

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that in history too, the generation of Moshe Rabbeinu was the 'head' of Klal Yisrael, a gathering of heads, and the generations descend until ikvesa diMeshicha, the 'heels', which, like the sole of the foot, have little sensitivity to lofty feelings. He says this generation will be transformed into the head, and uses the mashal of a fern, whose every branch is a small copy of the whole.

title.en: Space, time and Adar's hiddenness

summary.en: The Mashgiach shows the same structure in space, where the earth has a head, heart and lower parts, and in time, where Nissan is the head of the months and Adar the lowest, the month of hester panim, as the Gemara finds Esther in 'I will surely hide My face' and the Megillah has no name of Hashem and no open miracles. Our era is the 'Adar' of history, and he returns to the Tanya's words on the souls of the Avos and of ikvesa diMeshicha, adding that each individual also contains different levels.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that Zos Chanukah, the eighth day, seals the judgment of Yom Kippur and corresponds to Moshiach, and that it is a time to hope for the redemption and to daven.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens by saying that on Zos Chanukah, the last day of Chanukah, a simple Jew can achieve through prayer what a tzaddik achieves on Rosh Hashanah. It is accepted that this is the time of gmar chasima tova, when the sealing of Yom Kippur ends, and the eighth light corresponds to Moshiach. There is an obligation to await Moshiach at every moment; at the judgment one is asked whether he hoped for the redemption, and 'for Your salvation we hope all day', said three times daily, gives the answer. The Rambam speaks of awaiting, not only believing. He then reads the Yalkut about the year Moshiach is revealed, when the kings of the nations provoke one another and Israel is told not to fear. He concludes that Jews must daven, since prayer can annul decrees, and asks everyone to say l'chaim with gmar chasima tova.

en: What a tzaddik can achieve through prayer on Rosh Hashanah, a simple Jew can achieve on Zos Chanukah.
It is accepted among Jews that Zos Chanukah is the time of gmar chasima tova, when the sealing of Yom Kippur comes to its end.
Zos Chanukah, the eighth light, corresponds to Moshiach, so it is a time especially suited to hoping for him.
There is an obligation to await Moshiach at every moment, and one is asked at the judgment whether he hoped for the redemption.
The Yalkut describes the year Moshiach is revealed as a time when the kings of the nations provoke one another, and Israel is told not to fear.
Jews must daven, since prayer can annul decrees, even harsh ones.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that Shabbos is Hashem's personal gift to Klal Yisroel, and that a Jew must prepare for it all week, through tefillah, kedushas habris, guarded speech, learning its halachos and honoring its food, in order to feel it.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the Gemara that Hashem called Shabbos a good gift from His treasury and told Moshe to make it known, and explains with the parable of a chasan's flawless diamond that Shabbos is a personal sign between Hashem and Klal Yisroel. He then shows that the whole week revolves around Shabbos: every mitzvah and tefillah prepares for it, a Jew should long for it, and its fire must be kindled during the week. He teaches that Shabbos is reached through kedushas habris, that erev Shabbos is the day of Yosef and yesod, and that people who do not feel Shabbos did not prepare for it. He describes how the whole Shabbos davening, the seudos and the fish must feel like Shabbos, that Shabbos is a name of Hashem and is emunah, and that it must be guarded in speech. He closes with learning hilchos Shabbos and the holiness of Shabbos food.

en: Shabbos differs from every other mitzvah: it is a personal gift and a sign of the bond between Hashem and Klal Yisroel, and a Jew must know its worth.
All the mitzvos and tefillos of the week revolve around Shabbos and are a preparation for it.
Kedushas habris, guarding the mind and the eyes, is what brings a Jew to feel the holiness of Shabbos.
Those who do not feel Shabbos have not prepared for it during the week with kedushah and Torah.
Shabbos must be guarded in speech, because Hashem's work in creation was through speech.
The food of Shabbos carries great holiness, the holiness of the mann, and must be eaten in honor of Shabbos.

title.en: Shabbos, the gift from Hashem's treasury

summary.en: The Mashgiach opens with the Gemara that Hashem told Moshe He has a good gift in His treasury called Shabbos and that he should make it known, and asks why only Shabbos needed this. He answers with the parable of a chasan who sends his kallah a flawless diamond and must tell her it is not glass: Shabbos is a personal sign between Hashem and Klal Yisroel.

title.en: The whole week revolves around Shabbos

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that every mitzvah and tefillah of the week prepares for Shabbos and that a Jew should long for it like a chasan and kallah await the chuppah. He tells of chassidim leaving a melave malka at dawn who were greeted with the news that in six days it will be Shabbos again, recalls the European question whether a Jew 'has for Shabbos', and reads 'lo s'vaaru esh' as a call to kindle the fire of Shabbos during the week.

title.en: Praying for Shabbos; kedushas habris

summary.en: The Mashgiach says a Jew should pray constantly to merit a bright Shabbos and its oneg, and mentions R' Aharon of Karlin's song of longing for Shabbos. He teaches that the holiness of Shabbos is reached through kedushas habris, guarding the mind and the eyes in a world sunk in impurity, and that a warm Shabbos is a sign that one withstood such a test.

title.en: Erev Shabbos is the day of Yosef

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the six weekdays correspond to six sefiros and that erev Shabbos is Yosef, middas hayesod, through which one prepares for Shabbos. He brings Chazal that Yosef kept Shabbos in Mitzrayim, describes the 'bechinah of Yosef' as a Jew careful about what he eats, and says that one sunk in kelipos cannot feel Shabbos, as people complain to him.

title.en: Preparation and the Shabbos tefillah

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that one does not feel Shabbos because one did not prepare all week with kedushah and Torah. He brings the Panim Yafos that the whole Shabbos Shemoneh Esrei, not only its middle berachah, and the whole davening must feel like Shabbos, a tzaddik's teaching that at Nishmas one davens with the soul alone, and that teshuvah, from which the name Shabbos comes, brings a Jew close to Shabbos.

title.en: The Shabbos seudos; Shabbos as Hashem's name

summary.en: The Mashgiach says one eats all week to have strength to learn and daven and so to taste the Shabbos seudos, and tells of an old chassid who asked Hashem to give him Shabbos in the challah and in the fish. He brings the Zohar that Shabbos is a name of Hashem, so ehrliche Yidden avoid saying the word in an unclean place, explains that Shabbos is emunah, and urges davening to guard Shabbos.

title.en: Guarding Shabbos in speech; the Shabbos home

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains from the passuk that Hashem rested on the seventh day that His work in creation was speech, so a Jew must guard Shabbos by measuring his words and not talking business at the seudos, but Torah, stories of tzaddikim and a word on the sedra. He describes the Shabbos home, kavod habayis, and the Shabbos lights as honor and shalom bayis.

title.en: Hilchos Shabbos and the holiness of Shabbos food

summary.en: The Mashgiach urges learning hilchos Shabbos, at least from kitzurim, and seforim on the greatness of Shabbos such as the Sidduro shel Shabbos. He describes how ehrliche Yidden have in mind the holiness of Shabbos in every spoonful, tells of R' Dovid Biderman eating a spoiled cholent rather than shame Shabbos food, says the food of Shabbos holds the holiness of the mann, and closes with a gut Shabbos.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains the three ascending stages of Shabbos, culminating in Shabbos mincha and shalosh seudos, a time of yichud beyond place and time, and says one must want and pray to truly feel Shabbos.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the three parts of Shabbos: Friday night, Shabbos morning and Shabbos mincha, which parallel the three parts of the Beis Hamikdash and the stages of kiddushin, nisuin and yichud. Each part has its tefillah and its seudah, and the Avos come as guests to our seudos, so the table should be run to please them. Mincha is the highest point: its Amidah has no pesukim, its seudah is simple, and it is a 'nachalah without boundaries'. Through a question of the Avnei Nezer about the manna kept in the Kodesh Hakodashim, he shows that what is beyond place is beyond time, and so is shalosh seudos. The time itself is a mikveh, Moshe Rabbeinu passed away then, and the Ba'al Shem Tov had it eaten together. He ends with the mashal of the weary traveler, the story of R' Shlomo of Karlin's sock, and the call to want to feel Shabbos.

en: Shabbos has three stages, Friday night, Shabbos morning and Shabbos mincha, like the courtyard, the Heichal and the Kodesh Hakodashim, and like kiddushin, nisuin and yichud.
The Avos come as guests to the three seudos, so the seudah should be conducted to please the guests, with divrei Torah, joy and warmth.
Shabbos mincha and shalosh seudos are beyond place and time, the yichud of Hashem and Klal Yisrael, like the Kodesh Hakodashim.
The higher the kedushah of Shabbos, the less it is felt, so Friday night is felt most and mincha least.
One must want to feel Shabbos and ask Hashem for it; keeping Shabbos without trying to feel it leaves a person like a wooden bench in Gan Eden.

title.en: The three stages of Shabbos

summary.en: Citing the Nesivos Shalom, the Mashgiach divides Shabbos into Friday night, Shabbos morning and Shabbos mincha, compares them to the three parts of the Beis Hamikdash and to kiddushin, nisuin and yichud, and explains that each tefillah prepares for its seudah.

title.en: The Avos as guests at the seudos

summary.en: From the Zohar the Mashgiach links the three seudos to Yitzchak, Avraham and Yaakov, who come as guests, and says the table should be run for the guests: divrei Torah, simcha, and a warm, relaxed atmosphere the children can enjoy.

title.en: Mincha without pesukim, a portion without bounds

summary.en: The Mashgiach notes that the three Shabbos Amidos differ: Friday night and morning contain pesukim, but mincha is short and has none, because it is above pesukim; shalosh seudos is likewise a simple meal, and the Zohar ties it to the 'portion of Yaakov', a portion without boundaries.

title.en: The Avnei Nezer on the manna: beyond place and time

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Avnei Nezer's question how the jar of manna could be kept before Hashem when manna may not be left over till morning, and his answer that place and time are one: the Kodesh Hakodashim, where the Aron took no space, was beyond time too. Shalosh seudos is likewise beyond time until bentching.

title.en: Yichud, the Kodesh Hakodashim and the mikveh of time

summary.en: Shalosh seudos is the yichud of Hashem and Klal Yisrael, like the Keruvim in the Kodesh Hakodashim where no one else may be. The Mashgiach asks why no tevilah is mentioned before Shabbos mincha and answers that the time itself is the mikveh, as on Yom Kippur; Jews together are a mikveh, which is why the Ba'al Shem Tov had shalosh seudos eaten together. Mincha is the chosen time of Shabbos and an eis ratzon.

title.en: Brich Shmei, Moshe's passing, and feeling the kedushah

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the heavens open when the Aron is opened, above all at Shabbos mincha, and that Moshe Rabbeinu passed away at Shabbos mincha, a place beyond human measure, so no one knows his burial place. He brings the Toldos Yaakov Yosef that shalosh seudos alone is like weekday, and explains why the higher kedushah of the morning and of mincha is felt less than Friday night.

title.en: The taste of Shabbos and the weary traveler

summary.en: Like the manna, Shabbos tastes according to one's desire for it. The Mashgiach brings the Slonimer tzaddikim's mashal of a soaked, freezing traveler who reaches a warm inn to regain strength, as Shabbos restores a person for the week's avodah, and explains that time and place set the worth of a mitzvah, so Torah and mitzvos on Shabbos are of another order.

title.en: R' Shlomo of Karlin's sock, and wanting to feel Shabbos

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells how R' Shlomo of Karlin felt that his foot in a weekday sock did not feel Shabbos, and his warning that one who keeps Shabbos without trying to feel it will be like a wooden bench in Gan Eden. He speaks of gathering on Friday night to sing, of Klal Yisrael as the partner of Shabbos, of the difference between oneg and simcha on Shabbos, and closes with a tefillah before Shabbos Chazon.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains, through the image of an embryo whose hair and nails form last yet carry the same essence as the brain, the Tanya's teaching that even the lowest souls of Klal Yisrael stay bound with a wondrous bond to their first Source.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens on Rosh Chodesh Shevat, the day Moshe Rabbeinu began to explain the Torah, and says every Jew who learns is joined to Moshe by a thread. Returning to Tanya chapter 2, he restates the question of how souls that are all a part of G-d can differ in level, both between people and within one person's nefesh, ruach, neshamah, chayah and yechidah. He builds the Tanya's answer on the development of a child: the brain forms first and the hair and nails last, after nine months, yet the same essence runs through all of them. So too some souls are near to Chochmah Ila'ah and some are as distant as the nails, yet all are bound to their root. He applies this to cutting nails before Shabbos, to the Mishnah on those without a share in the World to Come, to Achan and the word Yisrael, to the calendar where Adar and the heels of Moshiach are the hidden 'nails' of time, and finally to the Tanya's switch from 'madreigos' to the Aramaic 'dargin'.

en: Every soul of a Jew is a part of G-d, yet souls differ greatly in level, between people and within each person's five levels of soul.
In a child, the brain forms first and the hair and nails last, but all develop from the same drop and carry the same essence.
Some souls are close to the supernal Chochmah like the eyes to the brain, and some are as remote as the toenails, yet all remain bound to their first Source.
No Jew is ever truly cut off from Hashem; being cut off exists only in theory, as the 36 kerisos and the Mishnah on the World to Come show.
The heels of Moshiach, like the month of Adar, are the 'nails' of time: the most hidden and remote stage, just before the birth of the Geulah.
The Tanya's switch from the Hebrew 'madreigos' to the Aramaic 'dargin' shows that even souls sunk as low as Targum are still bound to their root.
